href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+mechanic+shop+back+office+claustrophobic+afternoon+daylight+blocked+straw+hat+on+desk&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fryan_big_ticket_deal%2Fn2_shop_office_blind_down.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern mechanic shop back office claustrophobic afternoon daylight blocked straw hat on desk</a></div></div><p>The office was a room about the size of Marge's office and more cluttered. A desk with a computer that was four years out of date. A filing cabinet with a motor-oil stain at the top corner. A window that looked out on the work bay, which was why Ryan had a roller blind on it and the blind had been down since Tuesday. He had pulled it on Tuesday off-hand, as if for the sun, and she had watched him do it and had not asked why.</p><p>The farmer came in behind her. She closed the door. She turned the little latch she had shown herself how to use on a Tuesday in the third week, when she had come in to put the mail on Ryan's desk and had been alone in the office for a minute and had tested the latch because she was the kind of girl who did that now, which was a thing she had let herself register at the time and had not said out loud to anyone.</p><p>The farmer stood with the hat in both hands. He turned it once — the straw under his thumb the way a rosary was turned. She watched him not-knowing what the next line was supposed to be. She had not known either, until she had. The knowing came up out of her — not from Ryan having coached her, not from a script she had rehearsed. It came out of the four months of counting and the seventeen Saturdays of small closes and the long quiet that had been sitting between her and Ryan for three weeks now, which was a quiet with weight in it and which the afternoon on the gravel had not resolved and which, she registered, was not going to be resolved in this office either.</p><p>She took the hat out of his hands. She set it on the corner of the desk, where he could see it, where he could know that she knew it was his. She did not say anything. She did not have to.</p><p>It took what it took. She did not describe, to herself, the taking of it. She was aware of the blind being down and the clock on the wall going at its clock-speed and the particular weight of a man who had not been young for some years, and she was aware of her own body being the thing he was paying for, which was a thing she had agreed to be and had set the price of with the closing of the door. The price was the thing. She kept the price in her head through the length of time the taking took, the way a cashier at a register in town kept a number in her head between scanning the item and reading the total off the screen. The number did not move.</p><p>After, he counted the money onto the desk. A stack of twenties. He used the back of his thumb to separate them. He did it slowly because the counting was the thing he had to be able to do slowly, so that he could be a man who had come to buy a tractor again, on the way out. Two thousand even. He did not look at her while he counted. He slid the stack across.</p><p>She put the money into the manila envelope Ryan kept in the top drawer of the filing cabinet. She had put envelopes in that drawer herself, three Saturdays ago, in a stack, for exactly this. She moved two hundred and fifty dollars — twelve twenties and a ten from the bottom of the stack — into the small front pocket of her jeans before she sealed the envelope, and she was aware, as she did it, that the counting-twelve-twenties and the counting-a-ten was Maya-the-waitress's arithmetic, and that Maya-the-waitress was still the one running the count on a Saturday afternoon in Ryan's shop office with the blind down.</p><p>The farmer picked the hat up off the desk. He set it back on his head. He said, quieter than he had spoken in the yard, "Thank you, miss." — and she saw the shape of his face as he said it, which was the face of a man who had put the hat back on in order to walk out into the afternoon as a man who had bought a tractor, and she gave him the walk-out.</p><p>She stepped out of the office first. She turned the latch back off. She held the door for him. He went out into the customer area. At the door to the yard he touched the brim of the hat once at her without looking at her, and he went out onto the gravel, and she heard the Ford start and back up and turn and pull out onto State Route 9.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "8adf3053-fdde-45a2-bbd4-afdcd5700f83">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "beed400a-8d25-4f38-ba66-8db438cfbf7b">> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("ryan_big_ticket_deal.the_back_office") === -1) { vn.push("ryan_big_ticket_deal.the_back_office"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Set the envelope on Ryan's desk. over engine ignoring woman passing through back door envelope</a></div></div><p>She took the sealed envelope to Ryan's desk in the office and set it under the paperweight he kept on the stack of invoices — a piece of black iron the shape of a small anvil, which he had found on a job in Decatur three years ago and which he used for the stack because it weighed what it weighed. The envelope sat flat under it. She closed the office door behind her without locking it this time.</p><p>She went to the small sink at the back of the customer area, where Ryan washed his hands when he came in off the yard. She washed her hands. The water came cold first and then hot the way the pipes in the shop worked. She did not look up at the small square mirror above the sink, because the thing the mirror had to say was not something she needed to hear this afternoon.</p><p>She walked back through the customer area. At the door to the work bay she stopped for one count — not the count of deciding whether to go through, because that had been decided between the sink and the door, but the count of knowing that the going-through was going to be the sentence the going-through was.</p><p>Ryan was under the Cub. The shop smelled the way the shop smelled on a Saturday afternoon — engine oil and warm rubber and the back-of-the-yard grass Frank had mowed that morning, that was coming in on the draft through the bay door.</p><p>He did not look up.</p><p>She walked past him. She walked slow enough that he would have seen her if he had been going to see her, and he did not. The socket in his hand did not stop. The set of his shoulders did not change. The head-down was the sentence. It was the only sentence he was going to give her for this afternoon.</p><p>She walked through the bay. She walked out the side door. She did not set the hand on the other hand. The twelve twenties and the ten were in the front pocket of her jeans. The ninety-five from the diner the night before was on the dresser under the lamp in her room. The two numbers were in her head at the same time. They made the number she had needed them to make.</p><p>She sat with her hand on the wheel for a count of three. The heat through the windshield. The cicadas. A crow in the pines at the back of the lot.</p><p>She had taken money from a man for a thing she had given him. She had set the price of the thing before he had, and she had not moved it. She had walked past Ryan and Ryan had been the one who had not looked, not her. She started the engine. The Civic coughed and caught. hallway late night yellow nightlight one door ajar</a></div></div><p>She had been awake when the house cycled into its one-a.m. quiet. She had been awake because the window in her room was open and the cicadas were still running their August run even with September turned over on the calendar, and because she had been lying in the dark without trying to sleep, and the not-trying had been its own kind of work.</p><p>She got up. She did not turn on the lamp. She had been mapping Frank's upstairs hallway with her eyes closed since the second week, and the map was reliable enough by now that she could walk from her door to the bathroom door without the runner under her foot surprising her.</p><p>The hall was dark the way the hall was dark at one a.m. — the stair-top nightlight throwing yellow against the runner for three feet at the top of the stairs, and nothing past that. The house made the sounds a house made at one a.m.: the refrigerator, the settle of a floor-joist, the cicadas through the window at the end of the hall.</p><p>Jake's door was cracked.</p><p>She registered the door before she registered why she was registering it. The strip of light inside the gap was the low one — the desk lamp, not the overhead.</p><p>She slowed.</p><p>The sound that had been a house-sound a second ago separated itself. A pencil. The small quick scratch of a pencil on paper. She had grown up around a mother who had been a charcoal-drawer before Maya was born, and she knew what a pencil on a tooth-paper sounded like when the hand moving it was working not doodling. She knew the sound of work. She had been hearing it, or she had been hearing it without hearing it, since she had left her room.</p><p>She came level with the crack. lamp late night art student bedroom doorway view dim</a></div></div><p>The desk was in the far corner of the room under the one dormer window. The lamp on the desk was the desk lamp, a gooseneck brass one with an old paper shade, and the light from it was the kind of light that pulled the edges of things out of the dark without lighting anything else in the room. Jake was at the desk with his back half to the door.</p><p>He was in a black t-shirt, the sleeves hitting him above the elbow. His glasses were on. His hair was pushed back off his forehead because he had pushed it back with the inside of his wrist sometime in the last ten minutes and the wrist-push was still holding, the way a wrist-push did on his kind of hair for a while before the hair fell forward again. He was hunched slightly. His right hand was moving.</p><p>The page on the desk was wide-format, not his sketchbook. It was the heavier paper, the good paper, the tooth-paper she had watched him buy at the general store on a Thursday in August when he had paid cash from a folded bill and had not said hello to her even though she had been two aisles over.</p><p>The page had a woman on it.</p><p>The woman was most of the way drawn. The woman was sitting up in a bed with one knee drawn toward her chest and the other leg flat, the weight of her on one hip, her hair in the angle of a thing that had just been let down. The lamp beside the bed in the drawing was the little ceramic lamp from Maya's room — the one Diana had put on the nightstand the day Maya arrived, the one with the small chip on the base at four o'clock. He had drawn the chip. He had drawn the exact angle of the chip.</p><p>The woman's face was the face Maya had seen in the bathroom mirror on Tuesday morning while she brushed her teeth and thought about Frank's office and how the office smelled, which was a thing she had been thinking about on Tuesday mornings for two weeks. The mouth was her mouth. The angle of the jaw was hers. The shoulders were hers. The faint mole at the collarbone was hers. He had drawn the mole.</p><p>She did not breathe in for a count.</p><p>She stepped back. She did it quietly. She did it without letting her weight come down on the runner at the spot where the runner was thin over the floorboard that creaked. She had mapped that board two weeks ago. She stepped around it the way she had learned to.</p><p>He did not look up. The pencil kept moving.</p><p>She walked to the bathroom. Tonight the mirror was a thing she was not going to consult. She had been looked at. The looking had been done for her. The face in the mirror was not the face that needed checking.</p><p>She stood with her back against the door. The tile under her feet was cold. The hum of the bathroom fan was off; she had not pulled the cord. The window over the bathtub was cracked the same two inches every bathroom window in Frank's house was cracked at the end of summer, and the cicadas came through it the way they came through the window at the end of the hall. The small green tick of the wall clock above the medicine cabinet was the loudest sound in the room.</p><p>She let herself think about what she had seen.</p><p>He had been drawing her. He had drawn the chip in the lamp and the mole at her collarbone. He had drawn from memory, or from looking — she did not know which, and the not-knowing was a piece of the information now, and the information was hers. He did not know she had seen. He was on the other side of the hall with his glasses on and his pencil moving, making a woman on a page, making <em>her</em> on a page, and the him of tonight on the other side of the wall was not yet the him of tomorrow when he would sit at breakfast and not look at her and not know that she knew.</p><p>The two ways to do what came next were in the room with her.</p><p>She could step back from this door. Walk the hall back the way she had come. Close her own door behind her. Carry the knowledge into the part of her days that was hers and nobody else's. He would not know she knew. The not-knowing would be a thing she owned.</p><p>Or she could go back down the hall. Push his door wide. Stand in his doorway in the strip of his lamp-light and wait for him to look up, and let him see her seeing. The room would be the kind of room a room became when both people in it knew what had just happened, and the knowing would be a geometry she had made and not found.</p><p>The second way was a Maya who had not been all the way in the bathroom a minute ago.</p><p>She looked at her feet on the tile. She did not look at the mirror. Outside, a car on Route 9 changed gears for a hill. shop yard with older customer inspecting green riding mower</a></div></div><p>The Tuesday after the Tuesday Pete had bought the crankshaft was the Tuesday of the riding mower. The stool she sat on had become the stool — three Fridays and four Tuesdays since Ryan had handed her the pencil the ledger had been missing, and the stool had taken the shape it took for her hip and not for his. The box fan turned the air. The column-ruled spiral was open on the counter in front of her. She had filled six pages since the first Wednesday.</p><p>Pete came in at four-fifteen. He was in the dark-blue coveralls she had first catalogued at Marge's counter in May, and the Hayes Hardware cap had faded another shade in the weeks since, and his hands were clean at the knuckles the way they always were. He did not say hello to Ryan. He did not say hello to her. He said the mower outside, the green one, was Ryan selling it.</p><p>Ryan had been at the carburetor at the near end of the counter. He set the float bowl down. He stood up at the hip-crack, the way he stood up when something required him to stop what he was doing, and he stepped to the side of the stool she sat on. He did not speak. The Tuesday-nod Maya had learned by the second Friday came. She took the pencil. She took the ledger. She walked past him.</p><p>She walked with Pete out through the side door to the inventory yard. The riding mower was the John Deere that had been parked at the near-side of the fence line for six weeks — green paint oxidized at the hood, seat vinyl cracked at the left-side weld, chalk tag on the handlebar in Ryan's number-two pencil: 475. Pete walked the long side first. He put his hand on the rim of the wheel and rocked it. He tilted the seat back and looked under. He pulled the belt at the pulley with a finger and let it snap back.</p><p>He straightened up. He did not look at her. He looked at the hood. He asked the price without the verb.</p><p>She looked at him. She did not look at the chalk. The chalk was not the number.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> Four ninety-five.</div></div><p>She did not add because. Pete had the count she had watched him take at Marge's counter in the second week, the three-seconds-before-the-nod-or-the-not-nod count, and he took it and nodded once. He did not look at the chalk. He took the checkbook out of the inside pocket of the coveralls. He wrote the number. He tore the check. He handed it to her. She took it in her left hand. She did not look at it.</p><p>They walked back to the counter. She handed him the pencil. He signed the ledger. He handed the pencil back. He walked out under the roll-up door. His pickup door opened and shut. The engine turned over on the second crank. The sound thinned onto the county road.</p><p>Ryan had not said a word since Pete came in. He was at the stool again, the float bowl back in his left. He did not look up.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> Yeah. You got it.</div></div><p>He said it at the carburetor. The float bowl went back into the throat. Then he did look up, for the length of the count he held, and he broke it.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> Big one's coming Saturday.</div></div><p>He counted the thirty-five out of the drawer after the check went in, in fives, and slid them across the counter to her left hand the way he had slid the Gatorade across four Tuesdays ago. <em>Her cut.</em> She folded the thirty-five once and put it in the front pocket of her jeans. The asking-price was in the ledger; the over-ask was in her pocket. She wrote Pete's name and the mower and four ninety-five into the column on the next page, in the handwriting Ryan's handwriting had begun to defer to, on a page she had turned to before he did.</p><p>Saturday was three days away. The big one was not named yet. It would be named when it came. She would be at the counter at two.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "3e8b4f1c-6f8a-4ac5-bee4-a357f501dac6">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "e48cdf61-8ade-42b6-8cbd-bb4dae1894e6">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("3e8b4f1c-6f8a-4ac5-bee4-a357f501dac6");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("ryan_partner_first_close.base") === -1) { vn.push("ryan_partner_first_close.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(60);<</script>> <<script>>setup.pendingEffects = [];setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "money", "add", 35.0, false, null);setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "rep_road", "add", 3.0, false, null);setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("npc", "npc_ryan", "love", "add", 3.0, false, null);setup.showEffectNotification();<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "ryan_partner_open");<</script>> [[Fold the thirty-five into the front pocket. Key</div> <div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/marge_thursday_key/office_count_out.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A small cluttered back office in a diner at closing time — gray metal desk pushed against the wall, a gooseneck lamp pulled over an open ledger, a plastic cash drawer on the corner of the desk, a calendar two months behind on the wall, the door open to a dim kitchen pass behind.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=diner+back+office+at+night+closing+cash+drawer+open+ledger+gooseneck+lamp+gray+metal+desk&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_thursday_key%2Foffice_count_out.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 diner back office at night closing cash drawer open ledger gooseneck lamp gray metal desk</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=small+town+diner+owner+paperwork+pantry-sized+office+calendar+wall+cramped&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_thursday_key%2Foffice_count_out.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 small town diner owner paperwork pantry-sized office calendar wall cramped</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+roadside+diner+office+midnight+ledger+till+count+apron+on+hook&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_thursday_key%2Foffice_count_out.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern roadside diner office midnight ledger till count apron on hook</a></div></div><p>She brought the drawer back through the swinging door at the kitchen end of the pass at nine-fifty-one, which was the time the digital over the microwave had been showing when she turned the corner, and the time she had taken to mean nine-fifty-plus-slippage for most of the month. The drawer was the cash drawer — the plastic one with the slotted inserts for singles, fives, tens, twenties, and the fold-under slot where the checks lived — and she carried it two-handed, the way she had learned to carry it on her second Thursday after she had almost dropped it on her first.</p><p>Marge's office was a room about the size of a pantry. A gray metal desk pushed against the back wall, a filing cabinet with the second drawer that stuck, a wall calendar two months behind, a phone with a coiled cord that hung to the floor because the coil had given up some years ago. The gooseneck on the desk was on. Marge was under it, ledger open, pencil loose in her hand, not writing — reading the previous page the way she read the previous page every Thursday before she signed off on the current one. It smelled of old paper and cold coffee and the one cigarette Marge had on the back step at eight forty-five, carried in on her apron. Maya set the drawer down on the corner of the desk, on the felt pad where the drawer lived.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> Count it.</div></div><p>She counted it. The twenties first, by habit now — Cookie had told her on her second week that twenties first meant the mistakes showed up early and you had the rest of the count to find them — then the tens, the fives, the singles. The coin was already rolled; Cookie rolled the coin. The checks were three tonight, paper-clipped at the top because that was Marge's system and Marge did not have another one. Two hundred and fourteen dollars and sixty-two cents. She slid the drawer across. Marge ran her eye down it once, did not count again, and wrote the number in the ledger in the hand she kept for the ledger — block numerals, pencil, no comma.</p><p>The bell went off over the front door. Cookie came down the hall a second later with her denim jacket on over the t-shirt and her hair down for the first time of the evening, the high ponytail set loose at the office door. She stopped in the doorway with one hand on the jamb.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> I'm out. Fryer's down to one again, so Friday's gonna be a time. Maya — walk careful.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> Yeah.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Marge. Night.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> Night.</div></div><p>Cookie went. The front door bell went once more. The diner at nine-fifty-nine on a Thursday was the room it had been every Thursday since the hire — the lights on half, the grill ticking past the last heat, the line wiped, the back booths dark — except that tonight Maya had let herself register the fact that she was the one still in it.</p><p>Marge set the pencil down on the ledger. She did not close the ledger. She looked at Maya across the desk — the looking-without-making-eye-contact that was her version of attention, which Maya had figured out on her third shift and had stopped reading as indifference by her fifth.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> You're steady.</div></div><p>Maya did not answer right away. She had been in the office for a count of — she did the arithmetic later, walking home, and made it three — three seconds, before Marge said the next part.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> Thursdays are slow. Key's under the till.</div></div><p>She said it at exactly the volume and the clip of the first sentence. As if the two were one sentence that had a pause inside it that meant something to Marge.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> Lock the back when you leave. You good?</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> Yeah. I'm good.</div></div><p>Marge nodded once. She went back to the ledger. She picked the pencil up again.</p><p>The till was on the shelf above the desk where the till lived at night, drawer out and the till itself a plastic hollow that was not supposed to have anything in it. Maya lifted the box. The back-door key was underneath — small, brass, attached to nothing, the way Marge's one-key-per-door system ran. It had been sitting under the box, Maya realized, since Marge had put the till up for the count. It was room-temperature. She put it in the small front pocket of her jeans — not the apron pocket, because the apron was coming off in thirty seconds — and she felt the shape of the key settle into the seam at the bottom of the pocket against her thigh.</p><p>She took the apron off. She hung it on the hook by the office door.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> Night, Marge.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> Apron on the hook. You're good. Go.</div></div><p>She went out through the kitchen, through the back hall, and out the back door. She closed the door behind her. The key turned in the lock on the second try. It clicked. She pulled the knob. Locked.</p><div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/marge_thursday_key/walk_home_route9.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A dark rural two-lane at night — pine trees close at the shoulder, gravel where the paving ends, a single sodium-yellow streetlight in the middle distance at a crossroads, a young woman walking the shoulder alone with her hands in her jeans pockets.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=rural+two-lane+road+at+night+southern+pine+trees+gravel+shoulder+sodium+streetlight+alone+walking+home&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_thursday_key%2Fwalk_home_route9.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 rural two-lane road at night southern pine trees gravel shoulder sodium streetlight alone walking home</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=state+route+back+road+midnight+woman+walking+alone+small+town+cicadas+dark+pine&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_thursday_key%2Fwalk_home_route9.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 state route back road midnight woman walking alone small town cicadas dark pine</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=empty+southern+county+road+night+warm+humid+single+streetlight+walker+denim&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_thursday_key%2Fwalk_home_route9.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 empty southern county road night warm humid single streetlight walker denim</a></div></div><p>The diner lot ran up against the gravel at the side of State Route 9, where the shoulder narrowed from paved to gravel for three hundred yards at the edge of town before the paving picked up again past the old post office. She took the shoulder. She had taken the shoulder four Thursdays in a row now, and the walk was a walk she was beginning to know the way she had known the route to her high school — by its small distinguishings. The mailbox at the Deavers' with the flag still up. The cut-grass smell from the Hansens' that had been on them since Tuesday, when Mr. Hansen had been on the mower at six a.m. The single sodium-yellow light at the crossroads where Route 9 met the county road that ran out to Frank's. The cicadas on the last weeks of a long summer count, even with the season turning.</p><p><em>You're steady,</em> Marge had said. Maya heard it in her head at the clip Marge had said it — the two words at the even cadence, no lift under them, no warmth added and no warmth taken out. The compliment had landed at exactly the weight it had cost Marge to give. Maya had been running the arithmetic of Marge's costs for a month now. She let herself register the fact that she was running it.</p><p>She did not take the key out of the pocket. She walked with her hand in the pocket for the middle quarter-mile and then with her hand out. She passed the Hansens'. She passed the sodium light. She turned off Route 9 onto the county road where the dark got a degree darker because the lights were farther apart and the pines started. At the top of the drive she saw the porch light Frank had left on.</p><p>She had not decided yet what she was going to do with the Thursday. That would be a decision for the next Thursday. Tonight was the walking-home-with-it.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "55baa979-3556-410d-8443-b022091b0342">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "c7f08bfa-8eb8-471d-9012-5c62c6a9175d">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("55baa979-3556-410d-8443-b022091b0342");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("marge_thursday_key.base") === -1) { vn.push("marge_thursday_key.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(60);<</script>> <<script>>setup.pendingEffects = [];setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("npc", "npc_marge", "trust", "add", 5.0, false, null);setup.showEffectNotification();<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "first_ambient_tilt");<</script>> [[Walk the hour home. story/frank_phase_a_test/porch_rocker_dusk.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A front porch of a rural Southern contractor-built home at eight-thirty on a Sunday in early July — dusk still holding on the rosemary at the railing and the white of the far fence and the grass at the edge of the gravel, a fifty-year-old man in work clothes seated in a porch rocker with a folded newspaper on his knee and a lowball glass of Jim Beam on the boards at the edge where the rocker does not reach, a young woman sitting on the porch swing a few feet to his left with a dish towel on her shoulder, the porch light above them switched to off and the cicadas loud in the pines.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+farmhouse+front+porch+rocking+chair+dusk+man+with+newspaper+whiskey+glass+boards&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffrank_phase_a_test%2Fporch_rocker_dusk.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern farmhouse front porch rocking chair dusk man with newspaper whiskey glass boards</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=young+woman+on+porch+swing+summer+evening+cicadas+rural+southern+home&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffrank_phase_a_test%2Fporch_rocker_dusk.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 young woman on porch swing summer evening cicadas rural southern home</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=front+porch+Sunday+evening+screen+door+rocker+paper+Jim+Beam+lowball+glass+cicadas+pines&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffrank_phase_a_test%2Fporch_rocker_dusk.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 front porch Sunday evening screen door rocker paper Jim Beam lowball glass cicadas pines</a></div></div><p>She had come out onto the porch with the dish towel still on her shoulder because she had thought she was going to say she was going upstairs. The hour the light had gone out of the sky without turning the yard black yet — dusk held on the rosemary at the railing and on the white of the far fence and on the grass at the edge of the gravel — and the cicadas had started up in the pines a count ago, and Frank was in the rocker with the paper folded on his knee and a lowball of Jim Beam at the edge of the boards where the rocker did not reach.</p><p>She sat down on the porch swing. The chains took the weight in the creak they always took it in. He did not turn. He did not lift the paper. The whiskey was at the halfway mark in the glass — he had poured it thirty minutes ago, the way she had learned he poured on Sunday evenings, a finger past where Diana poured for him at dinner — and it had not gone down since she came out.</p><p>His jaw worked once. She had learned by now that the Frank-jaw-before-a-sentence was the first half of the sentence. The second half was the sentence itself. The sentence tonight was coming from the rocker, and it was going to land in the porch air between them, and it was not going to be long.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Maya.</div></div><p>He let the name land. He did not look at her. He let the cicadas have the count he needed and the count a second longer than that — the Frank-pause she had started to be able to read at the dinner table over the last two weeks. The pause was the part that was about him deciding whether to say the sentence the way he had decided to say it. The whiskey stayed at the halfway mark. His hand stayed flat on the folded paper on his knee.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> The porch light.</div></div><p>He did not turn after he said it. He did not drink. He did not unfold the paper. The correction was done. The porch was what it had been before the sentence, minus the shape the sentence had made in the air between the rocker and the swing.</p><p>That was the whole correction. Two sentences. The first was her name; the second was the object. There was no verb between them. He had built the sentence to not need one — the grammar that was the discipline, the discipline that was the position he ran the house from — and she had been in the house long enough now to hear the absence of the verb as the loudest part of the sentence.</p><p>The light. She knew the switch in the kitchen — the low oak toggle he had put in the week she moved in, the click on the downstroke the kitchen outlets did not have. The porch light he'd asked her not to leave on past midnight had been on, last shift-night home. He had seen it the next morning. He had not said anything at breakfast. He had waited until tonight. <em>That was the agreement,</em> he was not saying, and she heard the not-saying.</p><p>Three sentences were in her mouth at different distances from her teeth. One was the sentence Diana would have said if Diana had been the one to leave the light on. One was the sentence the Maya who had moved here in April would have said. And one was the sentence that was already on its way out of her body before the first two had finished being thought.</p><p>The cicadas were loud between them. The rocker kept its cadence. She had a beat before the beat would begin to be longer than a beat. The answer she gave was going to be who she was to him in the morning.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "f29167e6-a660-45a5-be5b-615ba477513a">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "91449e97-c5c2-41b4-ae37-f1d5a1b10a02">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("f29167e6-a660-45a5-be5b-615ba477513a");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("frank_phase_a_test.base") === -1) { vn.push("frank_phase_a_test.base"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "\"I forgot. 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A farmhouse kitchen at five-fifteen in the afternoon: butcher-block counter worn pale at the center with a pound of okra in a colander and green half-inch wheels cast-iron on the stove behind her, the refrigerator door just opened in the background with a young man in a black t-shirt at its open door holding a glass pitcher with a plastic lid, glasses pushed up into his hair.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=farmhouse+kitchen+butcher+block+counter+cutting+okra+window+above+sink+afternoon+light&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fjake_first_glance_noticed%2Fkitchen_pitcher.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 farmhouse kitchen butcher block counter cutting okra window above sink afternoon light</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+kitchen+late+afternoon+okra+prep+cast-iron+stove+woman+cutting+at+counter&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fjake_first_glance_noticed%2Fkitchen_pitcher.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern kitchen late afternoon okra prep cast-iron stove woman cutting at counter</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=young+man+in+black+t-shirt+at+open+refrigerator+holding+glass+pitcher+kitchen+afternoon&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fjake_first_glance_noticed%2Fkitchen_pitcher.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 young man in black t-shirt at open refrigerator holding glass pitcher kitchen afternoon</a></div></div><p>The kitchen at five-fifteen on a Thursday held the density of the hour before Diana served dinner — bacon fat and cooked-off water in the air, the fan over the stove on low, the refrigerator running in the background at the volume that could still be overheard under a knife-blade on butcher-block. Maya had been at the counter for forty minutes. A pound of okra in a colander at her elbow, half of it already sliced into the green wheels that Diana would fry in cornmeal on the cast-iron, because Thursday in this house was fried-okra night. The five chairs at the four-person table were set for five. Frank had added the fifth chair the day after she moved in.</p><p>Diana was at the stove with her back to the counter. She did not turn.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Thin enough, Maya.</div></div><p>Maya sliced the next piece thinner. The blade was tacky where the okra had opened the last piece against it. The window above the sink held the back yard at the hour the shadow of the oak had reached the rosemary pot, and the shadow had been, since the first week, a way for her to read the time without looking at the stove clock.</p><p>She heard him come in from the hallway before she saw him. She did not turn. Jake crossed the kitchen behind her without a hello — he had not said hello in four weeks, since the Sunday of the headphones and the half-sentence at the bedroom door — and his footfall went from hallway plank to linoleum to the front of the fridge in the cadence she had learned was his: shorter than Frank's, quicker than Ryan's, the weight on the balls of the feet instead of the heels. The fridge door opened. Its cold light was visible in the edge of her peripheral, below her chin at the counter.</p><p>He took the cold-water pitcher out. The pitcher was the glass one with the plastic lid that did not seat all the way on the rim. He had it in his hand, the lid tilted in the other hand, the glasses pushed up into his hair because he was not drawing, and he was lifting the pitcher toward his mouth when his hands stopped. Half a second. She did not look up from the blade. She knew the half-second because the fridge hum carried it, and because the glass lid did not click against the rim in the count where it would have if his wrist had been moving.</p><p>She caught, without turning, the edge of what his body did. The hair he had pushed back earlier with the inside of his wrist had fallen forward again, and he did not fix it. His t-shirt was black today. The pitcher stayed at the lip of his mouth half a breath past when it would have tipped. Then it tipped. He drank. He closed the fridge. He left. The hallway plank carried his footfall back toward his door.</p><p>Maya moved the knife through the next piece. Her hands were steady. The slice was thinner than the one before it, which was the thing Diana had asked for, and which was the only part of the minute before that she let herself register the edge of. She did not name what had happened at the fridge. She knew it had happened. The list she had been keeping since the second week was longer this Thursday by one row she was not going to write down. She had the row all the same.</p><p>Diana turned the bacon. The cast-iron hissed where a pocket of water had come up under it. The refrigerator resumed the volume it resumed when it was closed.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "27597ffe-e09b-4f2d-9390-bf6d1cf042bd">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "6e6393d5-efc4-4bf0-8465-3a9ce3f621a5">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("27597ffe-e09b-4f2d-9390-bf6d1cf042bd");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("jake_first_glance_noticed.base") === -1) { vn.push("jake_first_glance_noticed.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(20);<</script>> <<script>>setup.pendingEffects = [];setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("npc", "npc_jake", "love", "add", 2.0, false, null);setup.showEffectNotification();<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "jake_first_glance_noticed");setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "jake_noticed_open");<</script>> [[Finish the wheels. story/ryan_shop_first_visit/shop_counter_carb.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">Interior of a small rural equipment shop in the afternoon — plywood counter on stacked cinderblocks, a box fan on a folding chair, a small fridge of Gatorade at the end of the counter, a twenty-five-year-old man in a faded blue t-shirt on a stool at the near end of the counter with the pieces of a carburetor (float bowl, needle valve, jet) laid out on a grease-grey shop rag, a spiral-bound column-ruled ledger with a chewed pencil beside it, light angling in from a quarter-raised roll-up door.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=rural+small+engine+shop+interior+plywood+counter+carburetor+rebuild+parts+shop+rag&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fryan_shop_first_visit%2Fshop_counter_carb.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 rural small engine shop interior plywood counter carburetor rebuild parts shop rag</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+used+equipment+outbuilding+box+fan+Gatorade+fridge+afternoon+light+roll-up+door&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fryan_shop_first_visit%2Fshop_counter_carb.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern used equipment
