href="https://www.google.com/search?q=young+mechanic+rebuilding+carburetor+float+bowl+needle+valve+work+counter+faded+blue+t-shirt&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fryan_shop_first_visit%2Fshop_counter_carb.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 young mechanic rebuilding carburetor float bowl needle valve work counter faded blue t-shirt</a></div></div><p>The Saturday sun at three in the afternoon was the hottest thing about the day, and it had spread into the gravel between Frank's porch and Ryan's shop in a way that came up through her sandals. She had walked the fifty yards of the drive enough times now to know where the gravel ran deeper and where it thinned to red dirt. She had not walked it with this destination before.</p><p>She ducked under the quarter-raised door. The shop smelled of metal and grease and concrete gone summer-thick, slightly sweet from the Gatorades in the fridge, sharp at its edges with kerosene he'd been using earlier. A box fan turned the air without cooling it. The counter was a plywood slab on cinderblocks, and Ryan was on a stool at the near end of it with the pieces of a carburetor laid out on a shop rag that had started white and was not, now, white at all.</p><p>He did not look up. His hands did the work they had been doing when she walked in — the float bowl in his left, the needle valve in his right, his thumb seating the valve at a pressure the wrist had learned somewhere she had not watched him learn it. The scar across the back of his right forearm was visible above the rag. It was the scar from the yard two Sundays ago. Today's t-shirt was faded blue, not the grease-spotted white from the hood of the pickup.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> You lost?</div></div><p>She shook her head. She sat on one of the two metal folding chairs on the customer side. The ledger lay on the counter a foot from his elbow — spiral-bound, column-ruled, a pencil chewed at the eraser. She had let her eyes stay on the chewing for a second longer than she would have at Frank's desk.</p><p>A pickup rolled up in the gravel outside and the engine cut. A door opened and shut. An older man in a mesh-back cap with a feed-store logo worn nearly off at the brim came under the roll-up door and let his eyes adjust. Freshly shaved at the jaw and not at the neck, his work shirt pressed in the sleeve-lines his wife had put there that morning.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/customer_farmer.jpg" alt="The Retired Farmer" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>The Retired Farmer:</strong> Afternoon. Got a belt for a rear-tine tiller? Troy-Bilt, old one.</div></div><p>Ryan set the float bowl down. He did not stand up. He said the belt was in the inventory yard, eighteen dollars. The farmer said he had been getting it in Anniston for sixteen. Ryan said he could do seventeen. The farmer nodded once and walked past her chair to the side door. Ryan picked the float bowl back up.</p><p><em>The ten-percent dance.</em> She had heard Cookie name the Thursday trucker who tipped on the bill because his wife checked the receipts. She had heard Marge not ask at the register whether Maya was good at the count. The list she had been keeping since the second week was longer this afternoon by one row: the eighteen Ryan had asked for, the seventeen he had settled on without lifting his head from the carburetor, and the way the farmer would come back next Saturday because the drive to Anniston was an hour and this was down the road.</p><p>The side door opened and closed. The farmer's pickup started. Ryan did not look up when it pulled onto the county road. He finished the seat, set the needle valve beside the float bowl. He wiped his right hand. The scar on the forearm came out cleaner against the grey-black of the rag.</p><p>He looked up.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> You any good with numbers?</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> Yeah.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> Help me with the ledger tomorrow. I'll feed you.</div></div><p>She said yeah without the ceremony the question would have gotten in April. The ledger was not Frank's notepad in the drawer under the phone; it was a column-ruled spiral under a box fan. The columns ran the same way down the page. The artist part of her had already opened the first page without picking it up. Ryan nodded once at the fridge. She took a Gatorade. The bottle was cold in her palm in the way she was going to remember the shop by first.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "6216f715-3539-4024-b631-d0b2c6c695c7">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "bb18f2b1-a834-4f2b-8504-868dfeb72ce5">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("6216f715-3539-4024-b631-d0b2c6c695c7");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("ryan_shop_first_visit.base") === -1) { vn.push("ryan_shop_first_visit.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(60);<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "ryan_shop_first_visit");setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "ryan_help_tier_open");<</script>> [[Back across the gravel. Tomorrow, the ledger.->Location_Front_Porch]]<div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> Back Step <span style="opacity:0.7;">(cookie_peer_established)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> Cigarette</div> <p>Thursday at eight. The pass was clear for a count of three tables and Cookie unclipped the last ticket, wiped her hands on the apron front, and tipped her chin at Maya on her way to the back door. Maya followed. The back step was two concrete steps down off the kitchen and a strip of gravel to the dumpster and the sodium light at the corner of the back lot and the Route 9 shoulder past the chain-link. The screen door hissed and shut behind them.</p><p>Cookie sat on the top step, the way she sat the first smoke break of every shift — left elbow on left knee, right hand loose with the Marlboro already lit from the Bic she kept in the apron pocket. The phone came out and went back in; the older kid was asking when she was getting home, and she answered eleven, and she did not look up at Maya when she put the phone away.</p><div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] tier_c/cookie_peer_established/base_back_step.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">Thursday 8:00pm behind a small-town diner. Two concrete steps down off the kitchen screen door to a strip of gravel and a green metal dumpster. Cookie, mid-30s, blonde hair in a high ponytail loosened from the shift, sitting on the top step in a white cook&#x27;s apron over a faded t-shirt, cigarette in her right hand, left elbow on left knee. Maya on the step below her, dark hair pulled back, blue waitress apron, hands on her knees. Sodium light at the corner of the back lot casting orange across the gravel. Chain-link fence beyond, Route 9 shoulder past it. The back of the diner is cinderblock painted white, the DINER sign edge visible at the roofline.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=small-town+diner+back+step+smoke+break+waitress+cook+1980s+night&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=tier_c%2Fcookie_peer_established%2Fbase_back_step.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 small-town diner back step smoke break waitress cook 1980s night</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+diner+kitchen+back+door+cigarette+break+rural+sodium+light&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=tier_c%2Fcookie_peer_established%2Fbase_back_step.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern diner kitchen back door cigarette break rural sodium light</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=diner+staff+smoke+break+outside+night+gravel+dumpster+chain-link&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=tier_c%2Fcookie_peer_established%2Fbase_back_step.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 diner staff smoke break outside night gravel dumpster chain-link</a></div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> You gonna make it, new girl?</div></div><p>Maya sat on the step below her. The gravel under the step was the kind of gravel that looked red under a sodium light and black under the sun.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> I'm gonna.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Yeah you are. Hang a second, I'll tell you who's gonna tip you.</div></div><p>Cookie drew on the Marlboro. The drag was long and the exhale was away from Maya's face.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Thursday's trucker night. Dale's the one at the far stool, wedding ring, doesn't matter, tips on the bill not on the table because the wife checks the receipts. Bill lands at twelve. He'll round to twenty if you stand by his shoulder twice and refill the coffee. Don't stand by his shoulder if you don't want to. Marge'd give you the eight-top instead. Just so you know. Roy with the Peterbilt hat — eight to nine, meatloaf, tips in fives folded on the table. He's in love with his ex-wife's sister who lives in Nashville. Don't be anything at him. Coke-trucker's the same Thursday as Tuesday, you got him. Pete's Tuesdays only, he doesn't Thursday. Church couple Saturdays, Mill Street Baptist, they count the ice in the water and she says bless before the meatloaf. Don't clear anything until she's said it. I'm telling you so you don't embarrass Marge.</div></div><p>Maya listened. She did not write the names on the step. She would write them down later at her desk at Frank's with the fan on and the window cracked two inches and the pencil from the drawer under the phone. But she had them now — <em>Dale. Roy. The church couple. The Coke-trucker.</em> — and she had them because Cookie had decided to hand them over. The decision was a thing Cookie had made on Cookie's own time, and the handing-over was the sentence Cookie had not said, and the Marlboro burning in Cookie's fingers was the hour they were in.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Marge'll tell you, but I'll tell you faster.</div></div><p>Cookie ground the cigarette on the edge of the step, dropped the butt in the Maxwell House can filled with sand by the dumpster. She stood. Her back cracked once — goddamn — and she bent to pick up the apron ties she had loosened for the break, and she tied them again at the hip without looking.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> One more. Twenties first when you cash out. Mistakes show up early that way.</div></div><p>Maya stood. The cigarette smoke had gone into her hair and would still be there on the hour home. The smell was not unpleasant. It reminded her of someone she had not thought of since before the Sunday in April.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Alright. Back inside.</div></div><p>They went back inside. The screen door hissed and shut. The kitchen smelled of fryer grease and the Pine-Sol the floor had not yet been hosed with. Cookie was at the wheel before Maya had the apron re-tied at the counter.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "435aef95-d90c-46be-ad4a-20221c51a303">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "589ae051-3fd6-4169-9d88-d4777062f77c">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("435aef95-d90c-46be-ad4a-20221c51a303");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("cookie_peer_established.base") === -1) { vn.push("cookie_peer_established.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(10);<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "cookie_peer_established");<</script>> [[Back inside. Carry the names.->Location_Diner_Kitchen]]<div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> Regulars <span style="opacity:0.7;">(diner_rhythm_deepens)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> Shift</div> <p>The apron-knot was right now. She had tied it at the counter before the clock hit five and she had not looked down to tie it. Cookie had shown her that the second Thursday — string under the string, not over — and it had taken her three shifts to get it and a week past that to do it without her hands needing her eyes for the doing. The Tuesday was her seventh T0 and the first one she had walked in to without checking the chalkboard for the ticket count.</p><div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] tier_c/diner_rhythm_deepens/base_pete_coffee.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">Tuesday 5:18pm at the diner counter. Pete the mechanic in dark-blue coveralls and a faded Hayes Hardware cap at the second booth from the end, coffee mug already in front of him at his right elbow without his asking. Maya in apron behind the counter, hand still at the handle of the Bunn coffee pot on the warmer. Soft late-afternoon light through front plate-glass windows, the DINER sign in cursive red above the door visible in reverse through the glass. Six booths and six stools; the booth-numbering-by-floor-slope geometry established in first_diner_shift_t0.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=small-town+diner+counter+mechanic+blue+coveralls+coffee+mug+1980s+southern&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=tier_c%2Fdiner_rhythm_deepens%2Fbase_pete_coffee.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 small-town diner counter mechanic blue coveralls coffee mug 1980s southern</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=1950s-style+american+diner+booth+worker+coffee+natural+evening+light&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=tier_c%2Fdiner_rhythm_deepens%2Fbase_pete_coffee.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 1950s-style american diner booth worker coffee natural evening light</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=diner+waitress+apron+coffee+pot+counter+mechanic+customer+regular&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=tier_c%2Fdiner_rhythm_deepens%2Fbase_pete_coffee.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 diner waitress apron coffee pot counter mechanic customer regular</a></div></div><p>Pete walked in at 5:18. Tuesday was Pete's day. The dark-blue coveralls that lived folded in the back of his truck between jobs, the cap with the Hayes Hardware script in faded blue, the hands that were clean at the knuckles and would not be clean at the cuticles. He did not ask for coffee. She did not ask if he wanted it. The mug came down from the shelf above the till. The Bunn's third pot since five filled it. She set it at his right elbow at the second booth from the end. He nodded once. Pete was the nod-once kind.</p><p>She let herself register that she knew him. The knowing had not arrived all at once. It had come in Cookie's asides at the pass — Pete the mechanic, Tuesdays only, coffee and nothing, don't ask him about the wife — and in Maya's own watching of what he did with the coffee and how he did not add anything to it and how he laid the folded paper on the table face-down when he was through with the thinking he had come in for. <em>Pete.</em> She had not asked him his name. She did not need to. The name had come to her across a shift in three-second installments.</p><p>Others, too, now. The woman with the yellow folder and the crossword magazine, Monday and Wednesday mornings before the bank opened. The family in the booth by the door with the baby who wanted the extra napkins before the plate came, Saturdays at noon. The Coke-not-coffee trucker at the last stool, six o'clock Tuesdays, gone by six-forty because the shop floor opened at seven. She had the list of them now in the part of her head the Tuesday-shift went in. Cookie calling 'Order up' at the pass cleared the space where the name-list ran.</p><p>Cash-out at ten-oh-three. Forty-five at nine an hour for five, and seven on the table by Pete's mug, and the Coke-trucker's two, and the Saturday-family's three that was already a week old in the envelope Marge had paid out on Monday morning, and change. The seven sat on top of the stack. It was the first tip that had been a tip — a number that had been given on purpose, not rounded out of the pocket the receipt had come from. She counted it once. She slid it under the base. The fifty-two went into the apron pocket at her hip at the seam, the weight a clean small compact thing that had a shape now.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> You're good.</div></div><p>Cookie did not look up from the wheel to say it. The dishwasher made its small steady noise. Marge was at the register with her back to the floor, counting the drawer — the end-of-shift not-looking, the kind she had started doing the first Tuesday after Maya's second T0 and had been doing every shift since. The whole diner at ten smelled of what it smelled of by ten — coffee and bacon grease and the Pine-Sol Cookie had hosed the floor with at eight, the air cooling only slightly at the front where the glass was losing the afternoon heat. Maya hung the apron on the hook by the office door. The apron was starting to be hers. The hook was still Cookie's, and the hook was still Marge's, because the diner was not hers, because she had not earned the key yet.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "8e45061d-442f-49c3-9196-feaac83dd0e6">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "11ec0728-a41a-42d7-b231-4180b6faba04">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("8e45061d-442f-49c3-9196-feaac83dd0e6");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("diner_rhythm_deepens.base") === -1) { vn.push("diner_rhythm_deepens.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(300);<</script>> <<script>>setup.pendingEffects = [];setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "money", "add", 52.0, false, null);setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "hygiene", "add", -15.0, false, null);setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "rep_road", "add", 1.0, false, null);setup.showEffectNotification();<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "diner_regulars_named");<</script>> [[Hang the apron. Walk the hour home. Seven on top of the forty-five.->Location_Diner_Front_Floor]]<div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> The Math <span style="opacity:0.7;">(the_math)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> Desk</div> <div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/the_math/base_desk_calculator.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A teenage girl&#x27;s bedroom desk at nine-thirty at night in a southern farmhouse — lit only by a small ceramic nightstand lamp with a blue band at the base. A phone with a calculator app open on the wood desk next to a small stack of bills (ones, fives, one twenty) and a brochure folded to a page. An open notebook with handwritten figures. Window cracked two inches. Quiet late-summer interior.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=young+woman+at+bedroom+desk+at+night+with+calculator+on+phone+counting+cash+ceramic+lamp&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fthe_math%2Fbase_desk_calculator.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 young woman at bedroom desk at night with calculator on phone counting cash ceramic lamp</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=teenager+doing+budget+math+on+bed+desk+small+lamp+nightstand+blue+band+summer+night+southern&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fthe_math%2Fbase_desk_calculator.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 teenager doing budget math on bed desk small lamp nightstand blue band summer night southern</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=quiet+bedroom+at+night+calculator+phone+stack+of+bills+brochure+notebook+window+cracked+cicadas&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fthe_math%2Fbase_desk_calculator.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 quiet bedroom at night calculator phone stack of bills brochure notebook window cracked cicadas</a></div></div><p>The second Sunday she had been at the house was the Sunday she did the math. It was late — nine-twenty-eight by the alarm clock on the nightstand — and the house was at its Sunday-night register, which was Frank already up the stairs for the newspaper crossword and Diana at the sink rinsing the last of the glasses and the television off and the percolator off and the light under Ryan's door not yet on because Ryan had not come back from wherever the pickup had been since seven. The cicadas were already in their nighttime count. The oscillating fan on the dresser was off. She had clicked the ceramic nightstand lamp on, the one with the chipped blue band at the base, and the light it put on the desk was the light of a 40-watt bulb in a lamp with a shade that had been cream-colored once and was now the yellow shades got when they had been in a room that had had a summer in it.</p><p>She had her apron folded flat on the corner of the desk. She took the money out of the apron pocket. She put it on the desk. She took the money out from under the lamp — the cash she had put there on Friday night because putting it under the lamp had felt like putting it somewhere that meant she was keeping it — and added it to the stack. She counted it twice. She counted it the second time because the first count had been wrong in the direction she had expected it to be wrong, which was lower than her estimate. The second count was the same as the first.</p><p>A twenty. Three fives. Four ones. Nineteen dollars more in quarters and dimes from two days of tips and one breakfast she had not bought a coffee for. Thirty-eight ones in the stack from Wednesday and Thursday's shifts — which had been four hours Wednesday and five hours Thursday. Marge had her on the schedule for four shifts the next week, which was four more than the four she had done this week. She knew the bill in her pocket from the first paid Sunday was gone already. She had handed the first rent to Frank on the kitchen table this afternoon at three. Frank had taken it without counting in front of her and had written <em>Maya — Wk 1</em> on a small notepad from the drawer by the phone and had not said anything else about it.</p><p>She opened the calculator app on the phone. The phone was the same phone. The thumb already knew the math before the app did.</p><p>Rent was sixty a week. Summer was the summer — she had twelve Sundays left counting this one as paid. Sixty times twelve was seven-twenty. Personal things — a tube of the toothpaste she used, the kind of tampon the local pharmacy carried, a gallon of gas a week to go into town and back because the car was the car — she had put at ten a week. Ten times twelve was one-twenty. The tuition she had been carrying in her head since the phone call in April was fifteen hundred. Seven-twenty plus one-twenty plus fifteen hundred was twenty-three-forty. The total she needed to get to by the Monday before classes started, which was the third week of August, was twenty-three hundred and forty dollars.</p><p>She had, at the lamp, ninety-seven dollars and change. She had a schedule for four shifts at T0 next week and Marge had not yet committed to more. A T0 shift was forty-five. Four times forty-five was one-eighty a week gross. One-eighty minus sixty for rent and ten for personal was one-ten net. One-ten times twelve was thirteen-twenty. Plus the ninety-seven in front of her. Thirteen-twenty plus ninety-seven was fourteen-seventeen.</p><p>Fourteen-seventeen against fifteen hundred was eighty-three short. That was if Marge gave her four shifts every week for twelve weeks and she did not have a single unpaid day off and she did not have one flat tire and she did not have a pair of shoes give out and she did not have a single unplanned expense. Eighty-three short was the math for the version of the summer that did not have anything go wrong.</p><p>She wrote the numbers in the notebook. She wrote them once because writing them twice was the thing you did to be sure, and she had been sure at the first writing. The notebook was the black composition one she had brought from the apartment. The page was the first page she had opened it to in six weeks. Her handwriting on the page looked like her handwriting.</p><p>The college brochure was on the nightstand next to the lamp. It had been in the glovebox since Kentucky. She had taken it out yesterday and left it there. She had not opened it. She had seen the community-college sign on Main Street on Wednesday when the walk to the diner had taken her past the turnoff and had registered the sign without going to the building. She was not going to open the brochure tonight. She was going to leave it where she had left it. The brochure was not the part of the math that was in question.</p><p>She sat at the desk with the ninety-seven in front of her and the thirteen-twenty in the phone and the fourteen-seventeen in the notebook and the fifteen hundred that she had been carrying since April, and she did what she had been doing since she was eight and doing math at a table was a thing she did the way some other children learned to swim: she looked at the numbers and she let the numbers tell her what the numbers were saying.</p><p>The numbers were saying that the T0 column was eighty-three short in the best case, and that Marge's Tuesday comment — <em>Thursdays are different. We'll see about those.</em> — had been a piece of information Maya had heard without yet understanding what she was hearing. The Thursday shift paid more. The why of the paying-more had been in the way Cookie had said <em>if you can hold an eye</em> on her second day, off-hand on the floor between the pass and the counter, without explaining what the holding meant. The holding-an-eye had been a sentence Maya had filed at the back of the drawer at the time. The holding-an-eye was going to be a sentence she was going to pick up, tonight, and hold in the hand the twenty and the three fives were on the desk under.</p><p><em>There's more tier available if I want it. I can see where it goes from here.</em></p><p>She did not open the sketchbook. The sketchbook was on the desk — was under the notebook, actually, where she had put it two nights ago for no particular reason she had named to herself at the time — and the opening of it right now would have been the opening of the register that had drawn the flat-dumpling chicken and her mother's hands and the pine-log on the trail-head half a mile off the porch. The sketchbook was not the register the closing of the math belonged to. She left the sketchbook closed. She put the ninety-seven back in the stack. She put the stack under the lamp. She turned the lamp off. The house at nine-forty-one on a second Sunday in July did what houses did.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "bb79089e-a471-4ecd-8491-8063fb8df21e">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "5b51fa49-43a4-4952-a633-373d8e4c2268">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("bb79089e-a471-4ecd-8491-8063fb8df21e");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("the_math.base") === -1) { vn.push("the_math.base"); }<</script>> <<script>>advanceTime(60);<</script>> <<script>>setup.pendingEffects = [];setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "calculation", "add", 2.0, false, null);setup.showEffectNotification();<</script>> <<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "first_rent_paid");setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "group_settled_in");<</script>> [[Close the notebook.->Location_Maya's_Bedroom]]<div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> First Sunday <span style="opacity:0.7;">(first_sunday)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> Sixty for Frank</div> <div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/first_sunday/rent_envelope_kitchen_table.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A sunlit Sunday morning kitchen in a southern farmhouse. Three twenty-dollar bills laid side by side on a worn kitchen table, beside a small brown manila envelope with handwritten &#x27;Wk 2&#x27; in pencil on the front. A folded white waitress apron with hip stains hangs over the back of a wooden chair. On the counter behind, a Mr. Coffee percolator and a cast-iron pan with bacon grease cooling. A handwritten note on the back of an envelope tucked under a salt shaker. Window cracked behind the sink with morning light coming through and basil leaves visible on the sill outside.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=sunday+morning+farmhouse+kitchen+three+twenty+dollar+bills+on+table+brown+envelope+rent+payment+apron+on+chair&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_sunday%2Frent_envelope_kitchen_table.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 sunday morning farmhouse kitchen three twenty dollar bills on table brown envelope rent payment apron on chair</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=rural+southern+kitchen+rent+envelope+on+table+sunday+light+folded+apron+salt+shaker+handwritten+note&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_sunday%2Frent_envelope_kitchen_table.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 rural southern kitchen rent envelope on table sunday light folded apron salt shaker handwritten note</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=kitchen+table+morning+coffee+percolator+cast+iron+pan+bacon+grease+envelope+cash+basil+window+sill&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_sunday%2Frent_envelope_kitchen_table.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 kitchen table morning coffee percolator cast iron pan bacon grease envelope cash basil window sill</a></div></div><p>The note was on the counter under the salt shaker. Diana had written it on the back of the gas-bill envelope from Friday with the felt-tip pen she kept in the drawer by the toaster. The handwriting was the hand Maya had grown up reading on lunch-bag notes and refrigerator-door reminders for fourteen years before the apartment in Lexington and the year she had been on her own.</p><p><blockquote>Leave sixty for Frank before church. — D.</blockquote></p><p>She read it once. She read it twice. The reading-twice was the small pause her body had taken without asking, the way it had taken the small pause at the calculator app two Sunday-nights from now would also be a small pause it would take. She did not yet know that.</p><p>She had said <em>okay</em> to the rent at this same table eight days ago, in yesterday's clothes, with the coffee Frank had made still in the pot and the paper folded on the chair. She had not yet, then, understood that the saying-okay was the writing-into-the-ledger that the writing-into-the-ledger was. Sixty a week. Due Sundays. <em>That was the agreement,</em> Frank had not had to say, because the saying had been done.</p><p>The apron was on the chair where she had hung it last night when she had come in from the diner at twenty past ten with the cash stack folded once. She took the stack out of the apron pocket. She counted it on the kitchen table. She had not yet learned to count it twice the way she would learn to count it at the desk on the second Sunday two weeks from tonight; she counted it once and the count was correct because the count had been her own four-shift week and the math had not yet been hard.</p><p>Three twenties. She set the three twenties on the table side by side. The other ones and fives and the change went back into the apron pocket. The apron she folded along the apron-strings the way she had watched Cookie fold hers at the end of Cookie's Wednesday shift, which was the way the apron was meant to be folded if a person had been folding aprons for twelve years on a five-to-ten. Maya had not been folding aprons for twelve years. The fold was nearly right.</p><p>The brown envelope was in the drawer by the phone next to the small notepad on which Frank had written <em>Maya — Wk 1</em> with a number-two pencil last Sunday afternoon at three o'clock. She put the three twenties in the envelope. She wrote <em>Wk 2</em> on the front of the envelope in her own handwriting, which on the brown paper looked like her handwriting and not like Diana's. She set the envelope on the kitchen table at the place Frank's coffee cup would be when he came in.</p><p>Smell: bacon Diana had finished frying at seven-twenty and the cast-iron still smelling of it, coffee from the percolator, the basil from the side garden through the window cracked open behind the sink. Outside the cicadas were not yet at their day-count. From the porch the screen-door creaked once — Frank standing up from the rocker — and then the screen-door eased back to closed.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Maya.</div></div><p>Frank from the porch through the screen, at the volume of Frank speaking from the porch through the screen. He had said her name and had paused and had not yet said the rest.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Diana is going to walk to the service. You can walk with her. You can stay.</div></div><p>Three complete sentences, no contractions, the <em>you can stay</em> at exactly the volume of the <em>you can walk with her</em>. He had decided a long time ago how to offer a daughter her own mind. The note on the counter, the envelope on the table, the choice through the screen — Diana through Frank through the porch, the household of three sentences saying themselves at the same time on a second Sunday in July.</p><p>Maya looked at the envelope. She looked at the door.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "1822d23f-71e8-4c60-a240-fa902d685d79">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "a2e596ca-9c02-45fa-89dd-f220a766fd07">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("1822d23f-71e8-4c60-a240-fa902d685d79");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("first_sunday.rent") === -1) { vn.push("first_sunday.rent"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Walk to the service with Diana. "Location_Kitchen">><<script>>setup.pendingEffects = [];<</script>><<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyTrait("player", null, "money", "add", -60.0, false, null);<</script>><<script>>setup.applyAndNotifyFlag("player", null, "first_sunday_passed");<</script>><<script>>setup.showEffectNotification();<</script>><<script>>advanceTime(180);<</script>><</link>><br> <</nobr>><div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> First Shift <span style="opacity:0.7;">(first_diner_shift_t0)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> The Floor</div> <div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/first_diner_shift_t0/base_counter_trucker.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">Interior of a small-town diner late on a Wednesday evening, ~9pm. Long laminate counter with a row of stools, a Bunn coffee maker on a warmer plate behind the till, a fluorescent strip light over the pass. A young waitress in a white apron stands at the counter holding a glass coffee carafe in her right hand and a wet rag in her left, mid-pour over a man&#x27;s coffee mug. The man at the end stool is in his forties, sunburned at the neck above a t-shirt collar, beard, Caterpillar cap on the counter beside him; his hand on the cup is calloused and steady. The Coca-Cola wall clock above the pass reads nine-twelve. Booth in the background by the door has a family finishing pie.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=small+town+American+diner+late+evening+waitress+refilling+trucker+coffee+at+counter+Coca-Cola+clock+fluorescent+light&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_diner_shift_t0%2Fbase_counter_trucker.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 small town American diner late evening waitress refilling trucker coffee at counter Coca-Cola clock fluorescent light</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=diner+counter+at+9pm+long-haul+trucker+on+stool+sunburned+beard+Caterpillar+cap+young+waitress+with+coffee+carafe+Bunn+warmer&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_diner_shift_t0%2Fbase_counter_trucker.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 diner counter at 9pm long-haul trucker on stool sunburned beard Caterpillar cap young waitress with coffee carafe Bunn warmer</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=Wednesday+night+roadside+diner+interior+trucker+at+counter+end+coffee+refill+apron&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_diner_shift_t0%2Fbase_counter_trucker.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 Wednesday night roadside diner interior trucker at counter end coffee refill apron</a></div></div><p>The Coca-Cola clock above the pass said nine-twelve. The shift was five-to-ten and Maya was at the four-hour-and-change mark, which was the mark the dinner rush thinned to the second-coffee men — the count Maya had been watching for since Cookie had passed her at the pass at twenty past eight and tipped her chin at the clock without saying anything. The after-the-game family was finishing pie in the booth by the door. The trucker at the end of the counter had been at the end of the counter since seven, when his rig had been at the gravel turnout across the road.</p><p>She had figured out the booth numbers by the second hour — three by the window, two through eight running counterclockwise the way the floor sloped toward the kitchen wall and the way the booths had been numbered by someone forty years ago who had counted with the slope. She had learned the coffee pot — the Bunn behind the till was the regular, the second pot on the warmer was for decaf, the carafe in her right hand was the third Cookie had brewed since five — and the count of three swings from carafe to cup that meant the cup was half. She had learned that Marge wiped tables across not along, that booth three's salt-and-pepper pair sat on the inside edge of the table because that was where the man in the Caterpillar cap put it back when he was done, that the door bell rang at a different pitch when a regular came in than when a stranger did.</p><p>Smell: bacon and coffee and Pine-Sol, fryer grease bleeding through the swinging door from the back, the wet-rag of her own apron tied at the hip. Cookie had opened the kitchen door for the smoke break an hour ago and the smell of cigarettes from the back step had crossed the floor for the count of Maya standing in the middle aisle with two coffees in one hand. She had not registered the cigarette smell as a thing she would remember. She had registered it as a thing the diner had.</p><p>Cookie crossed the floor at quarter past nine on the way back from the kitchen pass, pulling the apron-strings tight at her hip as she walked. She did not stop. She said it past Maya's shoulder at the count of a woman moving plates from the pass to the counter — at the volume of a thing she had decided to say once and was not going to repeat.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> If you can hold an eye, that's the Thursday shift. Just so you know.</div></div><p>She did not wait for an answer. She did not turn her head. The two plates were down on the counter at booth two before the sentence had finished landing in Maya's head. Maya did not yet have anything to do with the sentence at the moment Cookie had said it, and she filed it the way she had been filing the things she did not yet know what to do with — at the back of the drawer, on the page she would come back to.</p><p>Marge had looked up once in the last hour to say <em>Two-egg brown for the counter, no toast,</em> without looking at Maya, and Maya had carried the plate before the words had finished landing. The carrying-without-thinking had been the small surprise of the night. The Bunn knocked itself on the warmer plate at the count it had knocked itself four times before. The fluorescent over the pass made the small steady noise it made.</p><p>The trucker at the end stool had been working a second cup of coffee for the count of two refills. He was forties, sunburned past the line of a t-shirt collar, the kind of beard a man kept because shaving on the road was a thing he did not do. His hands on the cup were the hands of a man who held a cup the way a man held a wrench when the wrench was at rest. Maya had registered his hands at the first refill, the way she registered hands. She had not yet, at the second refill, registered the rest of his face.</p><p>She came around the counter with the carafe in her right hand and the rag in her left. She stopped at his cup. She tipped the carafe. Three swings. She lifted the carafe.</p><p>He looked up.</p><p>The look was a beat longer than the look of a man being refilled by a waitress. It was a beat longer than the look she had felt across the dining room from booth four when she had carried the meatloaf past at seven-thirty. It was a beat longer than any beat she had counted yet — she did not have the counting of those beats yet — and she did not yet know what to do with the look.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Order up.</div></div><p>Cookie had set a plate down on the wheel without inflection. Marge at the till did not look up from the credit slips. The trucker did not break.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "d0dde96c-f965-442f-8a7b-33661da2b1a5">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "1998d256-372c-4b8e-ae91-11cec47a1e7e">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("d0dde96c-f965-442f-8a7b-33661da2b1a5");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("first_diner_shift_t0.base") === -1) { vn.push("first_diner_shift_t0.base"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Hold the look. an older woman with short iron-grey hair behind the counter counting out cash into the till drawer, a pencil behind her ear, a rag at her wrist; background a pass with tickets on the wheel, a young woman in a cook&#x27;s ponytail flipping a burger on the line.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=folded+white+diner+apron+on+laminate+counter+till+drawer+older+waitress+iron+grey+hair+counting+cash+afternoon&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_interview%2Fcounter_apron.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 folded white diner apron on laminate counter till drawer older waitress iron grey hair counting cash afternoon</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=small+town+diner+5pm+afternoon+float+count+apron+on+counter+cook+on+line+burger+ticket+wheel&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_interview%2Fcounter_apron.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 small town diner 5pm afternoon float count apron on counter cook on line burger ticket wheel</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=apron+on+counter+diner+new+hire+orientation+owner+counting+cash+young+cook+ponytail+grill&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Fmarge_interview%2Fcounter_apron.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 apron on counter diner new hire orientation owner counting cash young cook ponytail grill</a></div></div><p>She came in at four-fifty-nine by the clock on the wall, which she had been told by Diana that morning was the clock she needed to be inside of by five. The bell went over the door. The two men from Monday were at the counter on the same two stools, which Maya was going to learn, by the seventh shift, was how regulars sat. Marge was at the till counting out the morning float for the afternoon shift. She looked up.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> You came. Good.</div></div><p>The apron was on the counter in a folded square. It was a white apron of the kind a diner had been using since 1960 — faded at the tie from other people's knots, hip-stained, the ties longer than they needed to be. Marge pointed at it with the pencil she had been counting with.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/marge.jpg" alt="Marge" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Marge:</strong> Tie it. Learn as you go.</div></div><p>Maya tied the apron. She did not get the knot right on the first try — the ties were longer than she had expected, and she did it twice. Marge did not watch her do it. She was flipping a burger with a spatula and working a ticket on the wheel above the pass at the same time.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/cookie.jpg" alt="Cookie" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Cookie:</strong> Maya. Follow me two hours. You carry a plate when I hand you a plate. You take the coffee pot when I point at a table. You don't pour unless they ask for a refill. You ask me when you don't know.</div></div><p>Cookie handed her a ticket pad and a pen.</p><p>The next two hours were a pattern Maya had not had a pattern for. Booth one was Route 9 drivers. Booth three was an older couple with a regular order. The counter had the two men and a woman she had not yet seen. The coffee pot lived on the warmer by the pass. The till opened with a button under the lip. The pass was where tickets clipped and where Cookie set the food. The plates were heavier than she had expected. The carry against the hip was the carry Cookie showed her wordlessly, with the platter balanced above the hipbone on the forearm. By the second plate she had figured out the carry.</p><p>She did not spill anything. She put the right plate in front of the wrong person once, at booth three, and the husband said <em>This one's mine, honey</em> without looking at her, and she switched them without apologizing, because Cookie had told her in passing that apologizing was the thing that made the mistake stick. She had not known that. She wrote it down in her head.</p><p>At seven Marge walked the floor for five minutes and did not speak to her. At seven-ten Marge went back to the office. At seven-oh-eight Cookie had said <em>You're okay, kid</em> in a voice that was an evaluation, and had not repeated it. A mother in her late forties standing at the counter with a kitchen towel in her hand, having just wiped a spot that did not need wiping; her stepdaughter at the kitchen table behind her with a chipped Hayes Hardware mug in front of her on a worn oak table. Window over the sink cracked an inch, basil on the sill, percolator off but warm. The young woman is in jeans and a t-shirt with clean white sneakers on the floor by her chair, ready to leave.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+farmhouse+kitchen+monday+morning+mother+at+counter+towel+daughter+at+table+coffee+mug+percolator+window+basil&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ftown_walk_day_two%2Fkitchen_diana_route.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern farmhouse kitchen monday morning mother at counter towel daughter at table coffee mug percolator window basil</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=rural+alabama+kitchen+mid+morning+older+woman+wiping+counter+young+woman+seated+chipped+mug+oak+table&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ftown_walk_day_two%2Fkitchen_diana_route.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 rural alabama kitchen mid morning older woman wiping counter young woman seated chipped mug oak table</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+kitchen+interior+morning+light+percolator+stove+towel+counter+daughter+going+to+town+clean+white+sneakers&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ftown_walk_day_two%2Fkitchen_diana_route.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern kitchen interior morning light percolator stove towel counter daughter going to town clean white sneakers</a></div></div><p>Monday morning. The clock on the stove said nine-eighteen. Maya was at the kitchen table with the second mug of coffee Diana had poured for her without asking. Diana was at the counter with the kitchen towel in her right hand, wiping a spot she had wiped a count ago that did not need wiping a second time. Maya had been learning, since the Sunday she had come down the fourteen stairs in yesterday's clothes, that the wiping-of-the-spot-that-did-not-need-wiping was the thing Diana did when the thing Diana was waiting on was a person and not a pan.</p><p>Diana set the towel on the counter the way she set the towel on the counter when she had decided to say the thing she had been working out how to say. She turned. She did not look at Maya straight on; the looking-straight-on was reserved for things that had to be looked at straight on, and the route into town was not one of them.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Maya. Seven-tenths of a mile of gravel past the Hansens' and the Deavers'. Then the pavement past the old post office. Three blocks of Main Street.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> An hour at pace.</div></div><p>Naming the count was the kind of naming Diana did when she was telling Maya a thing without telling her a thing — which was that the thing had been taken seriously enough to count. The Hansens' and the Deavers' and the post office were on Diana's count by name because Diana had walked the road herself, with Maya's father, the spring after the wedding had been the first wedding, before Diana had been a woman with two husbands and a girl who had come down the fourteen stairs in yesterday's clothes a Sunday ago.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Frank can drop you.</div></div><p>It was an offer at the volume of an offer that did not need to be accepted. The mug was the chipped Hayes Hardware mug she had drunk the Sunday-morning coffee out of, and which had been at her place on the table every morning since. Diana picked the towel up off the counter and turned back to the counter. The wipe she had not finished was the wipe she finished now. The finishing was the closing of the saying.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "d47598a1-17fc-4606-a1a2-e799f56c5757">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "1fe14d0d-a84c-4aec-810e-18ed68e0a2f4">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("d47598a1-17fc-4606-a1a2-e799f56c5757");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("town_walk_day_two.kitchen") === -1) { vn.push("town_walk_day_two.kitchen"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Pick up the sneakers. white sneakers sun cicadas walk to town first time</a></div></div><p>She left at nine-thirty in the clean white sneakers she had not yet broken in. The road ran the way Diana had said it would — seven-tenths of a mile of gravel past the Hansens' and the Deavers', then the pavement at the old post office, then Main Street. The count had been a count Diana had given her in a tone Maya was going to learn was the tone of a thing Diana had walked herself before she had said it.</p><p>The gravel was red. Redder than the red she had remembered from the drive-through last August, the way the whole landscape had been redder than the landscape in her head. The pines started a quarter-mile off the drive and held for the next half-mile. It was already eighty-two degrees in the shade. The cicadas were on their morning count, which was louder than their noon count, which was a thing she did not yet know to expect.</p><p>Half a mile along, a pickup truck came up behind her in the opposite lane, slowed enough to read as slowing, and the driver — older, sixty maybe, brown ball cap, sleeve rolled — lifted one finger off the steering wheel in a flat, incurious hello. She nodded back without meaning to. Then she thought about the nodding. Then the truck was past her and gone in the dust off the gravel.</p><p>The pavement came up at the old post office, which was a cinderblock building with a padlock on the front door and Kentucky plates on a dead Ford in the side lot. The sidewalk came up after the post office. The three blocks of Main Street appeared past the white clapboard church on the corner.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "d47598a1-17fc-4606-a1a2-e799f56c5757">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "7ccfb20d-42f3-47ef-ad33-55080b780eb2">> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("town_walk_day_two.walk") === -1) { vn.push("town_walk_day_two.walk"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Walk up Main Street. booths formica counter pine-sol coffee smell iron-haired owner rag</a></div></div><p>Main Street was three blocks of brick: a Rite Aid on the first block, a hardware store and a lawyer's office on the second, the diner and a barbershop and an insurance agent on the third. The diner anchored the middle of the third block — a long low building with plate glass and a neon sign that read DINER in cursive red, unlit at ten-fifty in the morning because the sun was already full on it. A bell hung over the door. She went in.</p><p>It smelled like bacon and coffee and Pine-Sol. Six booths along the window, a counter with six stools, a pass at the back to the kitchen. Two men at the counter with coffees. A family in a booth by the door. bedroom door ajar strip of light studio headphones quiet house</a></div></div><p>Upstairs after dinner. The fourteen stairs in the bare feet she had not yet gotten used to, because at Frank's the floors were wide pine boards instead of the apartment's thin linoleum and they held the warmth of the afternoon through the evening in a way she had registered but had not yet named. The hall light was off. The stair-top nightlight was yellow on the runner, the same yellow it had been the first night.</p><p>Jake's door was the second door on the left between the bathroom and the room that was hers now. The door was open a crack — open two fingers wide, the way a door was open when a person had come through it and had not bothered to close it all the way, or when a person had set something against the jamb to keep it from closing. She did not know yet which kind of door-crack Jake's door-crack was.</p><p>The strip of light inside the crack was the low desk lamp throwing yellow. She could see him through it. He was at the desk in the corner with his back to the door, headphones on — the big studio kind, wrapped around his ears, cord running to a laptop. He was drawing or writing or both; she could not tell from the angle. His shoulders were set the way a shoulder was set when the person inside it was not interested in being interrupted.</p><p>She had been raised to say hello to people in a house she was going to live in for the summer. She had said hello to Diana twice that day and to Frank once, and the hello to Frank had been the whole exchange because Frank had looked up from the paper and had gone back to it. She had not yet said hello to Jake in a way that counted. The saying of it was still a thing she had to do.</p><p>She knocked. She did not push the door. She did it quietly, because she was going to close the door of her own room quietly tonight anyway — which was a thing Diana would not have asked for in so many words and which the whole of Diana's house had begun to teach her by being the kind of house it was. He was in a t-shirt that had been white some time ago, the sleeves hitting him above the elbow. He switched the wrench he had been using into his left and he put the new wrench on the bolt he had been trying to get and turned.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> Thanks, kid.</div></div><p>It came out the way he said things — one beat, no lift, the word <em>kid</em> filed flat against the thanks. She did not know whether to go or to stay. Staying meant staying on the gravel for however long he had the hood up, without a reason that was legible as a reason, because she had not come out here in the first place with a reason that was legible to herself and was not going to manufacture one now. Going meant going back into the house, where Frank was on the porch with the paper and Jake's door was closed as far as she knew and her own room was where it had been when she left it.</p><p>She watched his hand work.
