Soft early morning light through a window over the sink.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=southern+sunday+morning+kitchen+seven+am+father+at+table+with+newspaper+mother+at+counter&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_morning_kitchen%2Fbase_coffee_paper.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 southern sunday morning kitchen seven am father at table with newspaper mother at counter</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=rural+farmhouse+kitchen+percolator+sunday+breakfast+quiet+light+through+window+third+chair&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_morning_kitchen%2Fbase_coffee_paper.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 rural farmhouse kitchen percolator sunday breakfast quiet light through window third chair</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=family+kitchen+sunday+morning+coffee+paper+stepfather+older+woman+at+counter+early+summer&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Ffirst_morning_kitchen%2Fbase_coffee_paper.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 family kitchen sunday morning coffee paper stepfather older woman at counter early summer</a></div></div><p>She came down the fourteen stairs in yesterday's clothes. She had slept on top of the quilt with the jeans on and the t-shirt from the drive still on, and she had not opened the suitcase yet. The clock on the nightstand had said six-fifty-two when she had sat up. The house was already awake. The smell of coffee had been coming up the stairwell since somewhere before six-fifty-two, and had been part of what had woken her, and the other part had been the sound of the paper being opened at a table a man had been sitting at for already most of an hour.</p><p>The kitchen faced east. The light through the window over the sink was the light of a southern Sunday in July at seven in the morning, which was a light that had not yet decided whether the day was going to be the kind of hot that made the porch the cooler place than the kitchen or the kind of hot that made every room equally unusable by three. The percolator on the counter was going. The ticking of it was the ticking that had carried up the stairs.</p><p>Diana was at the counter. She had a coffee mug in her left hand and a kitchen towel in her right and she was wiping a spot on the counter that did not need to be wiped, which was a thing Maya was going to learn Diana did when the thing Diana was waiting on was a person not a pan. She did not turn around when Maya's foot hit the kitchen floor from the last stair. She had heard the fourteenth stair give before Maya had. She finished the wiping. She turned. She did not smile — the smile was reserved for a second later — and she looked at Maya for the count of a mother looking at a daughter who had slept in yesterday's clothes after a three-hundred-and-twenty-mile drive.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Sit.</div></div><p>Frank was at the table. He was at the end closer to the window with the paper folded open against the napkin holder, a mug at his right hand, the reading glasses that lived on the sideboard now on his face. He had looked up at Maya when she came in at the doorway and had looked back at the paper. The looking-back-at-the-paper was not rudeness; it was the register of a man giving a woman in his kitchen the count she was going to need to cross from the doorway to a chair without being watched for the crossing.</p><p>Diana slid a mug in front of the chair Maya had not chosen yet. The mug had <em>Hayes Hardware</em> on it in a faded blue block letter and was the mug Frank's lumberyard had given out at an anniversary three counties over that Maya would not learn the story of for another month. The coffee was stronger than what Maya made for herself out of the grocery can of Maxwell House; it was stronger than what Diana had made when Maya was small; the summer had put something into the mornings that the coffee had risen to meet. Maya sat. She held the mug. She did not drink yet.</p><p>Frank folded the paper. He took a long breath through his nose and let it out, which was a thing he did when he was about to say a sentence whose shape he had already decided on, and he looked up over the top of the reading glasses.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Maya. Rent's sixty a week, due Sundays.</div></div><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> You cook. Diana and I buy the groceries. That's the deal if you're staying.</div></div><p>Her mother had said no rent on the phone in April. Maya had known Frank would ask anyway, which was something she had known without having been told, the way she had known the shape of the ask before the ask had been made. She had done the math on it for most of Kentucky. Sixty was fair. Sixty was what a room would cost in a worse town and a worse woman for a landlord. The cooking was a thing her hands already knew how to do; Diana had taught them, before the move.</p><p>The fifteen hundred came into her head without her asking for it. Community college tuition. The number Diana had offered on the phone to cover. Maya was going to cover it herself. She was not sure yet how she was going to explain that to Diana. She was not sure yet whether she was going to.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-player"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/maya.jpg" alt="You" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>You:</strong> Okay.</div></div><p>Frank nodded, once, and opened the paper again. Diana at the counter did not turn around. The percolator ticked at the count percolators ticked at when the heat had gone off them and the coffee had settled.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Coffee's fresh.</div></div><p>A beat. The paper turned a page. Then the other thing.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Church is at ten. You can come. You can not.</div></div><p>He did not look up when he said it. The you-can-not was said at exactly the volume of the you-can-come, which was the register of a man who had decided a long time ago how to offer a daughter her own mind on a Sunday morning in a house where he was going to need her to know that he was not going to weigh the answer. The clock over the stove said seven-twelve. The light through the window had shifted a half-degree. Red-clay dust on the rear tire wells. Screen door of the porch starting to open. Cicadas implied by the angle of heat shimmer off the hood.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=rural+southern+gravel+driveway+farmhouse+Saturday+evening+late+afternoon+summer+car+arrival&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn1_car_on_gravel.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 rural southern gravel driveway farmhouse Saturday evening late afternoon summer car arrival</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=sedan+parked+on+red+clay+drive+in+front+of+two+story+southern+house+july+heat&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn1_car_on_gravel.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 sedan parked on red clay drive in front of two story southern house july heat</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=late+afternoon+arrival+at+family+home+gravel+drive+screen+door+opening+welcome&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn1_car_on_gravel.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 late afternoon arrival at family home gravel drive screen door opening welcome</a></div></div><p>The last mile of Route 9 had been the long one — pines tighter on both sides than she'd remembered from visits before the move, the radio dropped to one station that was a preacher at the end of his voice, the heat built up over four hours of interstate and one hour of county two-lane until the AC had stopped being a thing she could meaningfully adjust. The turn onto the drive came up on the left after the mailbox with the name she had not yet practiced saying in her own mouth. The tires took the gravel with a sound she remembered from somewhere older than this year.</p><p>She parked. She did not turn the engine off right away. The cicadas in the pines on the far side of the yard were into their five-in-the-afternoon count. Something frying in a neighbor's kitchen — chicken, or okra, or the particular Saturday smell of two of those together — carried across the far fence. The clay in the drive had dried to a red she had remembered wrong since the last visit: it was redder than memory.</p><p>The house was two stories. The porch had a rail that needed painting along the east half and didn't along the west. The screen door was a dark mesh through which the front hall showed as a stripe of cooler light. She kept her hands on the wheel. She had driven three hundred and twenty miles and was at the end of it, and the at-the-end was a thing she had been putting off recognizing the way she had put off recognizing the turn onto the drive until she was ten feet from missing it.</p><p>The screen door opened before Maya had turned off the engine — opened at the weight of someone who had been listening for the tires on the gravel since a quarter past four. The woman on the porch was her mother. The woman had been her mother for all of Maya's eighteen years, and she had been Mrs. Frank Hayes for five of them, and the standing-on-a-southern-porch was a new fact about her mother Maya had not sat with yet.</p><p>She turned off the engine. She put her hand on the door handle. She did not open the door for a count that was the count of a person needing one second more, and then she opened it.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "ba559314-82d0-4f27-9af5-e4e617a0cba1">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "952b0fd3-eb17-44a2-b35a-5e1b06c7673e">> <<script>>setup.markCanvasTriggered("ba559314-82d0-4f27-9af5-e4e617a0cba1");<</script>> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("arrival_at_franks.driveway") === -1) { vn.push("arrival_at_franks.driveway"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Get out." "Canvas_arrival_at_franks_Node_2">><<script>>advanceTime(2);<</script>><</link>><br> <</nobr>><div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> Arrival <span style="opacity:0.7;">(arrival_at_franks)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> The Porch</div> <div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/arrival_at_franks/n2_porch_hug_frank_doorway.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">A mother and teenage daughter hug on the steps of a two-story Southern farmhouse porch at late afternoon. Older man stands in the screen-door frame behind the mother, one hand on the jamb. Red clay drive visible in the foreground, an empty can on the porch rail, pines beyond.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=mother+hugs+teenage+daughter+on+southern+farmhouse+porch+late+afternoon+father+in+doorway&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn2_porch_hug_frank_doorway.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 mother hugs teenage daughter on southern farmhouse porch late afternoon father in doorway</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=reunion+hug+front+porch+summer+evening+stepfather+behind+mother+screen+door+frame&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn2_porch_hug_frank_doorway.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 reunion hug front porch summer evening stepfather behind mother screen door frame</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=arrival+welcome+southern+two-story+home+family+greeting+porch+steps+warm+golden+hour&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn2_porch_hug_frank_doorway.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 arrival welcome southern two-story home family greeting porch steps warm golden hour</a></div></div><p>Diana came down the two steps of the porch. She did not wait on the top step; she came all the way to the gravel. She was in a grey t-shirt Maya faintly remembered, jeans she did not, her hair pulled back with a pencil Maya had not remembered until this moment Diana put her hair up with a pencil when she was in the middle of doing something in a kitchen. The apron was gone — hung on the hook inside the door before Diana came to the porch. The basil-smudge at her hip was the tell.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Maya, honey.</div></div><p>The hug was on the drive, not the porch, and came with the weight of a hug that had been held back an inch for the length of the county two-lane. Diana smelled of laundry soap — the cheap grocery kind — and of basil from the side garden, and of something warmer than either that was in the skin of her neck behind the ear and had been Maya's mother's smell for as long as Maya had been old enough to register a mother-smell.</p><p>Maya hugged back at the weight of a daughter who had been three hundred and twenty miles on her own with the Prologue in her body. Diana read the weight — let the hug go another count than she would have otherwise — and did not ask. Diana was not the asking kind at this hour. She held Maya by the shoulders at arm's length, looked at her face, did not say what she saw there.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Come on in out of the sun.</div></div><p>Frank was in the doorway. He had come out of the kitchen at the sound of Diana's voice and had stopped at the jamb, one hand flat on it at shoulder height, the other in his pocket. He had shaved that afternoon. The face was the same face and was not; the line at the left corner of the mouth had been less deep the last time. He looked at her. He held the look for the count he held looks for.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Maya.</div></div><p>He said her name at the volume a man said a name at when the name was the full sentence he had to say. The two syllables landed at the weight of a stepfather acknowledging a stepdaughter on the day she crossed the threshold into the house where she was going to live. Not cold. Not warm. The sentence the moment required.</p><p>He came down the two steps. He offered his hand for the suitcase — offering hand as the sentence. Maya let him take it. The suitcase had been hers for the drive, and the handing-over was a thing she had not practiced and did it anyway. Frank took it at the handle the way a man took a suitcase from a woman who had driven three hundred and twenty miles: centered over his hip, not lifted shoulder-high. He turned toward the door.</p><p>Diana's hand was at the small of Maya's back, guiding her toward the steps. The hand did not push. The hand was there. The porch planks gave louder under her foot at the second step than the first. Diana reached past her to open the screen. The hinge sang. The inside of the hall was cooler.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "ba559314-82d0-4f27-9af5-e4e617a0cba1">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "35bb1720-0307-47fa-baa7-65898207bc2c">> <<script>>var vn = State.variables.game_state.visited_nodes;if (vn.indexOf("arrival_at_franks.porch") === -1) { vn.push("arrival_at_franks.porch"); }<</script>> <<nobr>> <<link "Inside." "Canvas_arrival_at_franks_Node_3">><<script>>advanceTime(3);<</script>><</link>><br> <</nobr>><div class="dev-canvas-info"><strong>Canvas:</strong> Arrival <span style="opacity:0.7;">(arrival_at_franks)</span> | <strong>Node:</strong> Hallway</div> <div style="border:2px dashed #666;padding:20px;margin:10px 0;border-radius:8px;background:#f5f5f5;"><p style="margin:0;font-weight:bold;color:#333;">[IMAGE MISSING] story/arrival_at_franks/n3_upstairs_hall_bedroom_door.jpg</p><p style="margin:5px 0 0;color:#666;font-style:italic;">Upstairs hallway of a two-story Southern farmhouse with a runner carpet, a bathroom door standing open across from a bedroom door, suitcase being set inside the bedroom, late-afternoon light through a hall window at the end. Warm domestic late-summer interior.</p><div style="margin-top:10px;"><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=upstairs+hallway+southern+two-story+home+bedroom+door+bathroom+door+runner+carpet+afternoon+light&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn3_upstairs_hall_bedroom_door.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 upstairs hallway southern two-story home bedroom door bathroom door runner carpet afternoon light</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=family+house+interior+upstairs+landing+late+afternoon+suitcase+at+bedroom+threshold&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn3_upstairs_hall_bedroom_door.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 family house interior upstairs landing late afternoon suitcase at bedroom threshold</a><a href="https://www.google.com/search?q=summer+southern+interior+hallway+wood+floor+runner+rug+warm+golden+light+through+window&amp;_tmc_game=output&amp;_tmc_scene=story%2Farrival_at_franks%2Fn3_upstairs_hall_bedroom_door.jpg" target="_blank" style="display:inline-block;margin:4px 8px 4px 0;padding:6px 12px;background:#3b82f6;color:white;text-decoration:none;border-radius:4px;font-size:13px;">🔍 summer southern interior hallway wood floor runner rug warm golden light through window</a></div></div><p>The hall ran front to back with the staircase on the right, the living room on the left, and the kitchen through the dining-room arch at the far end. Frank went up the stairs first with the suitcase. Diana stayed at the bottom with her hand on the newel post, looking up, not following. Maya counted the stairs because counting stairs on first climbs was a thing she had done since she was small. They were fourteen.</p><p>Frank turned left at the top. He set the suitcase inside the door of the second room on the left — the room Diana had told her about over the phone on the Sunday in April. A bed along the far wall with a quilt Maya recognized and a pillow she did not. A desk under the window. A chipped ceramic lamp with a band of blue at its base on the nightstand. An oscillating fan on the dresser, off. The runner in the hall ended at the door frame; past that the floor was bare wood.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/frank.jpg" alt="Frank" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["1e5b4a6f-d7d3-4495-bd4f-32131c454a8d"].name>>:</strong> Bathroom's across the hall. Dinner's at six-thirty.</div></div><p>Both sentences at the minimum length — the first a piece of information she could have found on her own, the second a piece of the ritual she was now inside. He set the suitcase down flat, not on its wheels, and stepped back into the hall. He did not close her door. He left it open at the angle a mother left a grown daughter's door when she was letting the daughter come to closing it on her own time.</p><p>He went down the stairs. The boards took his weight at a heavier count than they had taken hers coming up. From the window, before Maya had set her hand to any of the things in the room, a voice came up through the screen from the yard — through the two-inch gap the way voices carried on summer afternoons in the South.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/ryan.jpg" alt="Ryan" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong><<print $npcs["e34c78c8-4956-45b8-b021-737ced0d28a0"].name>>:</strong> Hey, kid.</div></div><p>Two syllables from a man who did not come inside to say them. A voice she would place later, on the second day, as Ryan's. Tonight she placed it only as a man's voice from a yard at arm's length through a screen. She did not go to the window. She did not answer. The voice was the sentence; the sentence had been said; the protocol was to let it have been said.</p><p>Dinner at six-thirty was in the dining room through the arch from the kitchen. The table was set for five. Diana at the head. Frank at the foot. Ryan was at the side of the table facing the kitchen — he had come in from the yard sometime between the suitcase going upstairs and the plates going on the table. She registered first his hands (on the table, knuckled and clean at the knuckle and tanned past it) and then the rest of him in the second pass. He said hey at the volume of a man who had already said it through a screen and was not going to repeat himself.</p><p>Jake was across from Ryan. Black t-shirt. Headphones around his neck, cord into the pocket of jeans older than Ryan's. Glasses off. He was looking at his plate before food was on it — the looking of a person who had chosen the plate over the room. Diana came to his chair and said his name once.</p><div class="dialog-block dialog-npc"><div class="portrait"><img src="./videos/diana.jpg" alt="Diana" onerror="this.style.display='none';this.parentElement.innerHTML='&lt;svg viewBox=&quot;0 0 100 100&quot; xmlns=&quot;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&quot;&gt;&lt;circle cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;35&quot; r=&quot;20&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;ellipse cx=&quot;50&quot; cy=&quot;85&quot; rx=&quot;35&quot; ry=&quot;25&quot; fill=&quot;#6c757d&quot;/&gt;&lt;/svg&gt;';" /></div><div class="dialog-content"><strong>Diana:</strong> Jake.</div></div><p>He nodded. He did not look up. The nod was the whole meeting — not rudeness exactly but the register of a boy who had decided the telling had been enough preparation. Diana served him. She did not say his name again.</p><p>Dinner was brief. The food was good. Nobody asked Maya about the drive. Frank asked Ryan about a part for the mower; Ryan answered in a fragment. Diana cleared before the table was empty. Maya was in bed by eight with her door closed. She closed it quietly. She lay on the quilt with her clothes on and listened to a house that was going to be her house — the percolator getting put away, the television at low volume in the living room, a truck down on Route 9 changing gears, the cicadas through her two-inch-cracked window — and the fact, which she did not yet have a name for, that she had crossed a threshold she was not going to cross back across.</p> <<set $game_state.current_canvas = "ba559314-82d0-4f27-9af5-e4e617a0cba1">> <<set $game_state.current_node = "922f1407-b960-46fa-b0a2-1fefeed21ddd">> <<script>>var vn = data-game-name="output"> <h2>The Long Summer — Prologue</h2> <p class="canvas-id-display">Canvas ID: <code>prologue_morning_with_daniel</code></p> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Sunday Morning</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-heading"><h3>Prologue</h3></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The apartment smelled like Daniel on Sunday mornings — his shampoo from the shower he&#x27;d taken before he came to bed, the specific wool of his weekend sweater on the chair, the ghost of coffee he hadn&#x27;t made yet because it was still too early. Maya kept her eyes closed and took inventory the way she always did when she woke up somewhere that wasn&#x27;t hers. Light against the eyelids: soft, morning, the blinds half-closed the way they had been closed last night. A car going past, two stories down. The building&#x27;s heating clicked and settled. Daniel&#x27;s breath against the back of her neck, not deep enough to be sleep, not awake yet either.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She had never told him she did this — lay in bed mapping the room before she opened her eyes. It felt like something she shouldn&#x27;t describe out loud, the way some private rituals felt more hers the less they were said.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>When she opened her eyes the ceiling was the same ceiling it had been for two years. A water mark in the shape of a comma by the vent. The paint around the light fixture a slightly different white than the paint on the rest of the ceiling, because the landlord had touched it up once without blending. She had asked Daniel about it during the second month of sleeping over and he had shrugged in the way that meant he had never seen it and did not intend to start. She had drawn the water mark in her sketchbook once — the comma, the faint halo of damp around it — and Daniel had asked her why she&#x27;d drawn something ugly. She had said it wasn&#x27;t ugly. He had said she was weird and kissed her shoulder.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She turned slowly. The sheet slid off her hip. Daniel was on his side, face pressed into the pillow, one arm flung over her stomach like he had been reaching for her in sleep and given up halfway. His mouth was open slightly. His hair did the thing it did in the morning. She had watched him sleep hundreds of times and she had not yet figured out how to draw the particular angle of his jaw when the muscles in it let go.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She put her hand against his hair. The gesture was so familiar she did not register it as a decision.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He made a sound — the not-quite-word he made when he was waking up, which was not a word in any language but which she would have recognized over a phone line in a country she had never been to. He moved his hand where it was on her stomach. He found the hem of her shirt. His thumb went under it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She watched his face come back to her. She loved this part — the specific minute between sleep and awake when the guard hadn&#x27;t come up yet, when he was only the weight of himself, and she was the first thing his hand was looking for.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>His eyes opened. He saw her. He did the small smile he did when the first thing he saw was her face, which he had done on every Sunday morning she had ever spent in this bed, and which she had never once watched without something quiet happening in her chest.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Hey.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>player:</strong> Hey.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Nothing was wrong.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The morning was just the morning.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Continue</li><li>Skip the prologue. (Go straight to Frank&#x27;s.)</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: The Slow One</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He kissed her. Not fully, not the way he kissed her at night — just a kiss against her mouth that was half a question, and when she answered by not moving away he kissed her again, more of one, the morning taste of him, the faint metal of last night&#x27;s wine still in the very back of his tongue.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Then he pulled back and looked at her again, because they had been together long enough that he asked her even when he wasn&#x27;t saying he was asking.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>player:</strong> Yeah.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>His hand was already under her shirt. He pulled the shirt up over her head and threw it in the direction of the chair where it would miss and land on the floor, which was a fact about Daniel and also a fact about their Sunday mornings. She reached for the waist of his boxers. They had done this enough times that neither of them bothered to be clever about it. The clothes came off with the efficiency of people who had stopped performing.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>His skin was warm from sleep. That was the thing about morning — he was not yet the person he would be at ten, when the coffee was in him and the edges came back. At eight thirty he was only warmth and the specific smell of the crook of his neck, which she had spent two years learning, which was his shampoo and his sweat and the laundry detergent his mother still bought for him and something underneath that was just Daniel, the thing that was him and no one else.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She pulled him onto her. He made the sound he made. She made the sound she made. The sheet tangled around their legs the way it always did and neither of them stopped to fix it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He was slow this morning. Some mornings he was fast — woke up wanting and did not negotiate with himself about it — and some mornings he was slow, and this was a slow one. His hand went to her jaw first, his thumb along the edge of it, the way he touched her face only when they were in bed. His mouth at her throat. His other hand finding the shape of her hip under the tangled sheet.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She closed her eyes. She did not close them to be anywhere else. She closed them because she wanted to feel it without watching — the familiar weight of him, the familiar way he knew where to put his hand, the familiar quiet of the morning around them that she had been inside every Sunday for two years and would be inside on this Sunday, and next Sunday, and the Sunday after that.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>That was the last thought she had like that.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She did not know yet that it was the last.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-video"><video src="./videos/prologue/n2_morning_sex.webm" autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="metadata" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;"></video><p class="media-caption"><em>Morning. Two figures moving together under a tangled sheet. The slow one.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>When he was inside her he said her name. Not moaning it — just saying it, the way he said it when he wanted to know she was there. She said yeah. She said yeah again. Her hand was on the back of his neck and his hand was still on the edge of her jaw and the sheet was a pale rectangle of kicked-aside fabric at the foot of the bed, and the morning light did the thing it did through the half-closed blinds, striping his back in slow parallel lines.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>It was not the kind of sex that went anywhere dramatic. It was the sex of people who had learned each other. He came first. He came saying her name again, pressed into her shoulder, and she felt it in her chest as much as her body. He stayed inside her a minute after. He kissed her temple.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> God, I love you.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>player:</strong> I love you.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She meant it. She had meant it that morning and for the whole weekend and for every week of the last two years, and she would go on for the rest of her life not doubting that she had meant it at that moment — and she would go on for the rest of her life knowing that he had, too, even while he was also meaning it, or some version of it, to someone else.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He rolled off her. He pulled the sheet back up over them both. He did the hair-smoothing thing he did to her hair afterward, absent, warm, the gesture of someone who was already falling back into the morning, into coffee, into Sunday.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> I gotta get up.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>player:</strong> In a minute.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> In a minute.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>They lay there. The heating clicked. A car went past.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Continue</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: The Third Door</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Wednesday was a Wednesday, and Wednesday was the last day of the semester. That was the thing she would remember afterward, the specific flatness of the day — the morning drawing class that had run five minutes long, the professor who had said *good luck, good summer* and meant it, the coffee she hadn&#x27;t finished, the hallway echoing in the particular way hallways echoed on the last week when most people had already packed up and gone home. A Wednesday in a life that had been, as of the morning she had spent in Daniel&#x27;s bed, perfectly shaped.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She had forty minutes before her last final, which was the Art History thing she was going to walk into and sit down and write for two hours and walk out of and not think about again until the grade came through in June. She had wanted to sketch.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The Fine Arts building was where she would normally have gone, but the studios were locked on finals week, and she did not want the whispered study-group sound from the lobbies. She walked across campus to the Humanities building. The third floor had six lecture classrooms, small ones, the kind they used for senior seminars and grad-student discussions, and on the last Wednesday of the semester most of them would be empty — which was, later, the detail she would keep stopping on, because if classes had still been running, none of this would have happened the way it did.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The third floor smelled like the photocopier down the hall that was always warm and the disinfectant they used on the handrails. She tried the first door. Locked. The second door. Locked. The third door opened.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The third door opened and she saw them.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-video"><video src="./videos/prologue/n3_classroom.webm" autoplay muted loop playsinline controls preload="metadata" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;"></video><p class="media-caption"><em>Fluorescent light. An empty classroom. A desk. Two figures she knows.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She saw them before they saw her. She had that — two seconds of seeing that belonged to her alone, that she would later parse and re-parse and be unable to give up, because the image was specific and complete and she was going to have to carry it: the fluorescent panel above the board flickering at the edge, the rows of empty chairs pushed in at the crooked angles students leave them, Sarah&#x27;s backpack — the olive-green one Maya had helped her pick out last fall at the thrift on Fifth — slumped against the leg of a student desk, Sarah&#x27;s sweater crumpled on top of it, Sarah&#x27;s skirt shoved up around her waist, Sarah on the edge of the professor&#x27;s desk with her knees apart and her hands braced behind her, Daniel between her knees with his mouth on hers and one hand in her hair in the particular way Maya had felt his hand in her own hair on Sunday morning.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Sarah&#x27;s mouth was doing the thing Sarah&#x27;s mouth did, which Maya had seen a hundred times in a hundred non-sexual contexts over three years of friendship — the slight left-sided hitch of her lips, the way she pressed her tongue against her teeth before a laugh — and which was now doing it for Daniel.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Neither of them looked up.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She stood in the doorway for somewhere between two and four seconds. She knew the count because later, in her apartment, she would try to reconstruct exactly how long she had stood there, and she would not be able to decide, and her inability to decide would become one of the things she carried.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Long enough to register that she was not misreading. Long enough to be sure she was not going to look back at this in an hour and wonder if maybe she had seen something else. Long enough that if either of them had glanced at the door, they would have seen her.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Neither of them glanced at the door.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She closed the door.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She closed it quietly. She did not slam it. The part of her that slammed doors had not been in the room with her, apparently, for some time — she had left that part of herself somewhere, maybe on Sunday morning, maybe earlier, and what was in her body in the third-floor hallway was the other part, the part that closed doors quietly, the part that would turn out to be most of her from here on out.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She walked down the hallway. She walked down the stairs. She walked out of the Humanities building and across the quad and past the coffee cart at the edge of the quad, and she sat on a bench outside the library because her legs had decided to sit before she had decided to sit, and she took her sketchbook out of her bag and put it in her lap.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She did not open it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She sat for fifteen minutes on the bench. A boy she did not know walked past with a dog she did not know. A bell rang somewhere. Her phone buzzed twice in her coat pocket and she did not look at it. The sun moved the specific amount the sun moves in fifteen minutes on a Wednesday in October.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She stood up. She walked back to the parking lot at the edge of campus. She got in her car. She drove home.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>In her apartment she locked the door behind her with the specific care of a person handling something breakable. She sat down on her bed with her coat still on.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Continue</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Item Four</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The laundromat&#x27;s dryers vibrated the floor at a frequency she had stopped hearing three weeks into her lease. She could hear it now. It was the sound of the afternoon agreeing with itself that nothing had changed, and the floor continued to hum, and the light came through her curtains the way it had come through last Wednesday&#x27;s curtains and the Wednesday before that, and she sat on the bed thinking very carefully about how not to cry.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She was not going to cry. That part she had decided on the bench.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>What she did not yet know was what the decision was instead.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She made a list, not on paper. On paper would have been an action, and actions meant commitment, and she was not ready to commit. In her head the list had items.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Item one: she could call him. She saw the version of herself that called him — the shape of that sentence, the way her voice would sound through the phone, the things he would say — and discarded it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Item two: she could confront them. Go back to the classroom, or to Sarah&#x27;s apartment, or to Daniel&#x27;s, and perform the shouting version of this, the slap, the thrown glass. The version of herself that did that was a version she could perform, had performed, at fifteen, at sixteen, a girl with a clean wound and a louder voice. The wound was not clean. She was not fifteen.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Item three: she could tell Kevin. Just call him, tell him what she had seen, let him break up with Sarah cleanly. The version of herself that did this was a good person. That self-knowledge was interesting — a good person existed in her, was in fact available on short notice — but she noticed that she did not want to become that person at this particular moment. She put the option down. The good person in her was very quiet.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She sat on the bed.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The sketchbook was on the desk. It had been open since the weekend to a page of Daniel&#x27;s hands — she had been drawing his hands on Friday evening while he watched a movie, the way she had drawn his hands a dozen times before, because she liked the particular knuckle of his left ring finger and the vein across the back of his hand that showed when he was cold. They were the blue-willow plates that lived on the top shelf of the left cabinet, the ones Diana had not put on the table since the Easter after the move. The napkins were the cloth ones, ironed flat. The iced tea was in the pitcher Diana brought out at company, not in the plastic jug the weekday tea came in. The overhead light was off and the pendant over the table was on, and the pendant had been on since Maya had come downstairs, which meant Diana had been at the table for longer than the dumplings had needed her. The kitchen smelled of chicken broth reduced down to the color of a low amber, of black pepper cracked that afternoon and not from the shaker, of the biscuit-flour kind of dough the flat dumplings were cut from before they went into the pot. The smell was not the usual Sunday smell. The smell was the Sunday-before-the-move smell, which was the smell of a kitchen Diana had learned to run as a wife, not as a widow remarried.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>*The flat kind, not the round.* The sentence arrived at the volume of a voice heard a long time ago in a kitchen in Tennessee. Maya&#x27;s father had said it every Sunday he had been able to say it, which had been the Sundays of her first eight years, and the saying had been part of the requesting and the requesting had been part of the routine, and the routine had ended on a Wednesday in her ninth year and had not been reassembled until this Sunday in this kitchen by this woman at this table. The flat kind, not the round. Diana had made them flat. Diana had cut the dough in strips with a knife and not with a glass. Diana had remembered.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Frank was at the foot of the table. It was not the chair the extra place setting was at.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The extra place setting was next to Diana&#x27;s, on Diana&#x27;s right, where the empty chair from the extra leaf of the table had been pulled up. The blue-willow plate at that place was face-up. The flatware was aligned. The cloth napkin was folded in thirds. The chair had been pulled out for her.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Diana came from the stove with the pot and set it at the trivet at the center of the table. She straightened. She wiped her palms on the apron. She looked at Maya — not at the face, at the hand Maya had on the back of the chair Maya had been standing behind for forty seconds without sitting.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Maya, honey. Set a place for yourself next to me.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The sentence was eleven words. It was the only full sentence Diana had said to Maya about anything that was not the grocery list or the laundry or the porch since the Monday in late May when Maya had carried her suitcase in off the drive. It was the sentence Diana had not said for four and a half months. It was the sentence Diana had been not-saying since the second week of July when the Thursday hour had started, and she had been not-saying it louder with each week, and the not-saying had been a discipline, and the discipline had been what made the saying of it tonight weigh what it weighed.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Maya moved to the chair on Diana&#x27;s right. She pulled it in. She sat. The chair she had been standing behind stayed empty; the chair across from Jake, which had been her summer chair, was not her chair now. Frank registered the move without looking up from the plate. Ryan registered it by putting down the glass. Jake registered it by putting the glasses in his shirt pocket the way he had put them in his shirt pocket the Saturday of the brothers-discover dinner. None of them spoke. The dinner was the dinner. The plates went around. Diana served the dumplings into each bowl with the ladle that belonged to the good serving set, which was the ladle that had not been on the table since Tennessee.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Maya ate next to Diana. Diana&#x27;s arm was warm in the space between them. The food was good. Maya had forgotten that her mother had been a cook before she had been a widow, and she had forgotten that the kitchen Diana had kept in the first house had been a different kitchen with a different arithmetic, and the remembering landed on the flat dumpling on the fork between her plate and her mouth and stayed.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Finish the plate.</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: The Doorway, the Coffee</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/keep_tier_fork/n2_doorway_coffee.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>An older woman turning in a kitchen doorway to look back at the table — soft Sunday-evening light, a table with dinner plates still on it, a younger woman seated at the head end. Diana always finished her plate before Maya did; Diana ate at the weight a woman ate at when she had been cooking since the men had come in from church at noon. She pushed back from the chair. She picked up her plate. She picked up Frank&#x27;s plate because Frank had finished. She picked up Jake&#x27;s fork because Jake had set it on the napkin. She did not pick up Ryan&#x27;s plate because Ryan was still eating.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She carried the plates through the arch between the table and the kitchen. Diana set the plates in the sink, not on the counter. She ran the tap for a second, not for rinsing — the running-for-a-second was the signal to the table that the dishes had not been started yet, they were going to sit a minute — and she went to the percolator.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She turned in the doorway before she went to the percolator. She stood in the kitchen doorway and she looked at Maya. She did not smile. She did not frown. She did not say anything. She held the look for the count of three, which was the count past polite by two counts, which was the count Diana did not hold a look for, which was a count Diana had not held a look for since June.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Then she turned back into the kitchen and the percolator came on and the water ran for real this time and the can of Maxwell House got opened the rest of the way and the scoop went into the grounds and the grounds went into the basket and the basket went into the percolator. The sounds were the sounds. The sounds were the sounds of a mother making coffee for two cups, because the Sunday coffee after dinner was Diana and Frank and Frank did not drink coffee after Sunday dinner unless Diana had made it for two cups specifically, which was the Sundays Diana wanted the second cup for herself.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The look had been the question Diana had not asked all summer. The question she did not want the answer to had become — at some hour of some day Maya had not been counting — the question Diana had decided she did want the answer to, and the wanting had become a thing Diana had been holding behind her not-asking, and the holding had filled up until the holding could not hold anymore, and the not-asking had come out on a Sunday night through the Maxwell House and the ironed napkin and the chair on her right and a single sentence said in daylight at a volume anyone at the table could hear, and then the not-asking had put itself back on — as the look, which was the form of the question when the woman asking it was Diana.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Frank did not stand. Ryan did not stand. Jake did not stand. The three men at the table were waiting to see what Maya did next, and each of them had a stake in what she did next, and each of them was sitting in the chair he was sitting in at the weight his stake put him at. Diana was in the kitchen making coffee. The catalog was done. She took the coffee pot off the warmer. She went back out onto the floor.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The rest of the shift was the rest of the shift. She did the tilt once more at the six-top by the door, because she had decided in the back hall on the way to the walk-in that she would do it once more and would clock the not-feeling again. She clocked it. The not-feeling was the same not-feeling. The tip on the six-top went six dollars over what the tip on a six-top of that composition would have gone without the tilt, and Maya registered the six dollars as the number that the tilt weighed, and she did not register anything else.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>At ten-forty she cashed out. The tips came to ninety-five dollars on the cash line, plus what was on the credit slips, which Marge would settle on Thursday next. She folded the ninety-five and put it in the small envelope she kept in the apron pocket for the folding. She took the apron off. She hung it on the hook by the office door.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Apron on the hook. You&#x27;re good.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Marge&#x27;s eye moved over Maya&#x27;s face and did not land. Marge did not ask if she was good. Marge had not asked if she was good in a number of shifts now, and Maya had registered the not-asking the first Thursday after the farmer and had known what the not-asking meant without needing to have it named.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She went out the back. The key turned in the lock on the first try — a brass key in a lock wore smooth to the shape of the lock by the fourth use, which was a thing Maya had learned in the last year about keys — and she pulled the knob and the door was locked.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She walked the shoulder of State Route 9. The cicadas were still running their long August count even in October, the calendar turned but the South on its own schedule. The Deavers&#x27; mailbox still had the flag up. The Hansens&#x27; grass was short because Tuesday had been a Tuesday. The sodium light at the crossroads was on. She passed under it without looking up at it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She did not think about what she was going to say to herself about what she had done on the floor, because the saying-to-herself-about-it was a thing Maya-of-August would have done. She put her hands in the front pockets of her jeans. The ninety-five was in the apron, and the apron was on the hook.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: location</em></div> </div> <div class="review-back-btn"> <<button "← Back to List">><<goto "CanvasReviewList">><</button>> </div> </div><div id="canvas-review-detail" data-canvas-id="ryan_big_ticket_deal" data-game-name="output"> <h2>The Back Office</h2> <p class="canvas-id-display">Canvas ID: <code>ryan_big_ticket_deal</code></p> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: The Thursday Before</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/ryan_big_ticket_deal/n0_shop_bay_gatorade.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A small rural shop interior, Thursday afternoon. Customer desk with a sale ledger open to a half-filled page; a young woman in a t-shirt and jeans seated at the desk with a pencil in her hand. The bay door open behind her — a young man in a cream t-shirt leaning against the door track with a yellow Gatorade bottle in his right hand and a three-quarter socket in his left, looking out at the gravel lot. Late-summer afternoon light, fan on the desk, the red tractor visible at the far edge of the gravel.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Thursday afternoon. The shop in the slow Thursday count — no customers since the morning truck-stop guy who had come in for a starter and left without buying it, and the next walk-in not until tomorrow at the earliest. Maya was at the customer desk with the sale ledger open to the page she had been keeping for Ryan since her second week — the running list of who had walked into the yard, what they had come in asking for, what they had walked out paying. He turned it again. Maya had been able to read the turning as the thing Ryan did with his hands when he was about to say something he had been thinking about.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Farmer&#x27;s coming Saturday. He&#x27;ll fold, he won&#x27;t know it till you tell him.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He said it without turning his head. The socket kept turning. He took the Gatorade to his mouth at the count he took the Gatorade to his mouth at, which was the count of a man who had been drinking Gatorade out of bottles since he was eight years old, and he tipped the bottle and swallowed and brought it back down and the bottle went to the middle finger and ring finger of his right hand the way he held it when he was not actively drinking it. He did not look back at her to wait for an answer. He took another swallow off the Gatorade and walked into the bay, and the rolling-door noise of his footsteps on the concrete covered the small click she made closing the sale ledger. Two-twenty by the shop clock, which was the clock on the tower over the IGA in town reflected backwards in the window of the office — Ryan had told her about it at the end of her second week and she had never needed to check a clock in the shop since. FOR SALE in marker on a sheet of printer paper, taped to the windshield. Two thousand four hundred. He had said it in one word — &quot;Farmer.&quot; — and Maya had known immediately what he meant, because by Week 7 she could hear his fragments in four layers and the farmer-layer was one of them. You&#x27;re askin&#x27; blood for this.&quot;</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Ryan was at the rolling door of the work bay, one hand on the door-track and the other holding a three-quarter socket he was not using. He turned the socket in his hand. He turned it again. Maya watched him do it and had, for some weeks now, been able to read the turning as the thing Ryan did with his hands when he was deliberately not filling a silence with his voice.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The farmer looked past him. At the threshold he stopped and pulled the straw hat off his head with both hands and held it in front of his waist and looked at her. He did not say anything. He waited.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She closed the ledger she had been pretending to keep. She stood up.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Step into the office. Close the door behind you.</li><li>&quot;Ryan&#x27;s in the bay. Talk to him.&quot; Walk out the front.</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: The Close</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/ryan_big_ticket_deal/n2_shop_office_blind_down.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A small cluttered shop office with a desk and an older computer, a filing cabinet with a motor-oil stain at the top corner, a window with a roller blind pulled fully down to the sill, a cream straw hat sitting on the edge of the desk, fluorescent overhead light on.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The office was a room about the size of Marge&#x27;s office and more cluttered. A desk with a computer that was four years out of date. A filing cabinet with a motor-oil stain at the top corner. A window that looked out on the work bay, which was why Ryan had a roller blind on it and the blind had been down since Tuesday. He had pulled it on Tuesday off-hand, as if for the sun, and she had watched him do it and had not asked why.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The farmer came in behind her. She closed the door. She turned the little latch she had shown herself how to use on a Tuesday in the third week, when she had come in to put the mail on Ryan&#x27;s desk and had been alone in the office for a minute and had tested the latch because she was the kind of girl who did that now, which was a thing she had let herself register at the time and had not said out loud to anyone.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The farmer stood with the hat in both hands. He turned it once — the straw under his thumb the way a rosary was turned. She watched him not-knowing what the next line was supposed to be. She had not known either, until she had. The knowing came up out of her — not from Ryan having coached her, not from a script she had rehearsed. It came out of the four months of counting and the seventeen Saturdays of small closes and the long quiet that had been sitting between her and Ryan for three weeks now, which was a quiet with weight in it and which the afternoon on the gravel had not resolved and which, she registered, was not going to be resolved in this office either.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She took the hat out of his hands. She set it on the corner of the desk, where he could see it, where he could know that she knew it was his. She did not say anything. She was aware of the blind being down and the clock on the wall going at its clock-speed and the particular weight of a man who had not been young for some years, and she was aware of her own body being the thing he was paying for, which was a thing she had agreed to be and had set the price of with the closing of the door. The price was the thing. She kept the price in her head through the length of time the taking took, the way a cashier at a register in town kept a number in her head between scanning the item and reading the total off the screen. The number did not move.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>After, he counted the money onto the desk. A stack of twenties. He used the back of his thumb to separate them. He did it slowly because the counting was the thing he had to be able to do slowly, so that he could be a man who had come to buy a tractor again, on the way out. Two thousand even. He did not look at her while he counted. He slid the stack across.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She put the money into the manila envelope Ryan kept in the top drawer of the filing cabinet. He set it back on his head. He said, quieter than he had spoken in the yard, &quot;Thank you, miss.&quot; — and she saw the shape of his face as he said it, which was the face of a man who had put the hat back on in order to walk out into the afternoon as a man who had bought a tractor, and she gave him the walk-out.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She stepped out of the office first. She turned the latch back off. She held the door for him. He went out into the customer area. At the door to the yard he touched the brim of the hat once at her without looking at her, and he went out onto the gravel, and she heard the Ford start and back up and turn and pull out onto State Route 9.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Set the envelope on Ryan&#x27;s desk. Walk through the bay.</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Past the Work Bay</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/ryan_big_ticket_deal/n3_work_bay_head_down.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A lean young man in a cream t-shirt and jeans leaning in over the open hood of an older blue Cub Cadet tractor in a shop work bay, socket in right hand, left hand on the fender, head down — the shop door to the customer area visible past him with a young woman walking through carrying a manila envelope, he does not look up.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She took the sealed envelope to Ryan&#x27;s desk in the office and set it under the paperweight he kept on the stack of invoices — a piece of black iron the shape of a small anvil, which he had found on a job in Decatur three years ago and which he used for the stack because it weighed what it weighed. The envelope sat flat under it. She closed the office door behind her without locking it this time.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She went to the small sink at the back of the customer area, where Ryan washed his hands when he came in off the yard. She washed her hands. The water came cold first and then hot the way the pipes in the shop worked. She did not look up at the small square mirror above the sink, because the thing the mirror had to say was not something she needed to hear this afternoon.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She walked back through the customer area. At the door to the work bay she stopped for one count — not the count of deciding whether to go through, because that had been decided between the sink and the door, but the count of knowing that the going-through was going to be the sentence the going-through was.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Ryan was under the Cub. The hood was up. He was leaning in over the radiator with a three-quarter socket in his right hand and his left hand flat on the fender. He had the cream t-shirt and the jeans and the scar on the back of the right forearm visible because he had rolled the sleeve past it an hour ago. The shop smelled the way the shop smelled on a Saturday afternoon — engine oil and warm rubber and the back-of-the-yard grass Frank had mowed that morning, that was coming in on the draft through the bay door.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He did not look up.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She walked past him. She walked slow enough that he would have seen her if he had been going to see her, and he did not. The socket in his hand did not stop. The set of his shoulders did not change. The head-down was the sentence. It was the only sentence he was going to give her for this afternoon.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She walked through the bay. She walked out the side door. She crossed the gravel to her Civic — the hundred-and-twenty-dollar Civic she had bought off a kid in Cookie&#x27;s neighborhood two months ago, the one with the door that stuck on the hinge side — and she opened the door and got in and set her right hand on the wheel. She did not set the hand on the other hand. The twelve twenties and the ten were in the front pocket of her jeans. The ninety-five from the diner the night before was on the dresser under the lamp in her room. The two numbers were in her head at the same time. They made the number she had needed them to make.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She sat with her hand on the wheel for a count of three. She turned the key of the radio off because the radio was on — the country station from the gas station two weeks ago — and she did not need it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She drove the county road home.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: location</em></div> </div> <div class="review-back-btn"> <<button "← Back to List">><<goto "CanvasReviewList">><</button>> </div> </div><div id="canvas-review-detail" data-canvas-id="jake_peek_discovery" data-game-name="output"> <h2>The Drawing</h2> <p class="canvas-id-display">Canvas ID: <code>jake_peek_discovery</code></p> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: A Pencil in the House</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/jake_peek_discovery/n1_hallway_door_crack.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A dim upstairs hallway at 1 a.m. — stair-top nightlight throwing yellow against the runner, a bedroom door cracked two fingers wide with a strip of lamp-light inside, everything else dark.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She had been awake when the house cycled into its one-a.m. quiet. She had been awake because the window in her room was open and the cicadas were still running their August run even with September turned over on the calendar, and because she had been lying in the dark without trying to sleep, and the not-trying had been its own kind of work.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She got up. She did not turn on the lamp. She had been mapping Frank&#x27;s upstairs hallway with her eyes closed since the second week, and the map was reliable enough by now that she could walk from her door to the bathroom door without the runner under her foot surprising her.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The hall was dark the way the hall was dark at one a.m. — the stair-top nightlight throwing yellow against the runner for three feet at the top of the stairs, and nothing past that. Diana was asleep at the far end. Frank was asleep in the master. Ryan&#x27;s door was closed. The house made the sounds a house made at one a.m.: the refrigerator, the settle of a floor-joist, the cicadas through the window at the end of the hall.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Jake&#x27;s door was cracked.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She registered the door before she registered why she was registering it. The door had been closed every other night she had walked this hall. Tonight it was not closed. The gap was two fingers wide. The strip of light inside the gap was the low one — the desk lamp, not the overhead.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She slowed.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The sound that had been a house-sound a second ago separated itself. A pencil. The small quick scratch of a pencil on paper. She had grown up around a mother who had been a charcoal-drawer before Maya was born, and she knew what a pencil on a tooth-paper sounded like when the hand moving it was working not doodling. She knew the sound of work. She had been hearing it, or she had been hearing it without hearing it, since she had left her room.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She came level with the crack. The strip of light threw a thin line across her bare feet and across the runner, and the line landed at the baseboard on the far side of the hall.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She did not mean to look.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Look.</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: The Chip at Four O&#x27;Clock</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/jake_peek_discovery/n2_desk_drawing_page.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A lean young man in glasses and a black t-shirt hunched at a small wooden desk under a gooseneck brass lamp, a large-format tooth-paper sheet in front of him, a pencil drawing of a seated woman mid-render on the page — seen from the hallway side, through a cracked door.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The desk was in the far corner of the room under the one dormer window. The lamp on the desk was the desk lamp, a gooseneck brass one with an old paper shade, and the light from it was the kind of light that pulled the edges of things out of the dark without lighting anything else in the room. Jake was at the desk with his back half to the door.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He was in a black t-shirt, the sleeves hitting him above the elbow. His glasses were on. His hair was pushed back off his forehead because he had pushed it back with the inside of his wrist sometime in the last ten minutes and the wrist-push was still holding, the way a wrist-push did on his kind of hair for a while before the hair fell forward again. He was hunched slightly. His right hand was moving.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The page on the desk was wide-format, not his sketchbook. It was the heavier paper, the good paper, the tooth-paper she had watched him buy at the general store on a Thursday in August when he had paid cash from a folded bill and had not said hello to her even though she had been two aisles over.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The page had a woman on it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The woman was most of the way drawn. The woman was sitting up in a bed with one knee drawn toward her chest and the other leg flat, the weight of her on one hip, her hair in the angle of a thing that had just been let down. The lamp beside the bed in the drawing was the little ceramic lamp from Maya&#x27;s room — the one Diana had put on the nightstand the day Maya arrived, the one with the small chip on the base at four o&#x27;clock. He had drawn the chip. She had walked the fifty yards of the drive enough times now to know where the gravel ran deeper and where it thinned to red dirt. She had not walked it with this destination before.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She ducked under the quarter-raised door. The shop smelled of metal and grease and concrete gone summer-thick, slightly sweet from the Gatorades in the fridge, sharp at its edges with kerosene he&#x27;d been using earlier. A box fan turned the air without cooling it. The counter was a plywood slab on cinderblocks, and Ryan was on a stool at the near end of it with the pieces of a carburetor laid out on a shop rag that had started white and was not, now, white at all.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He did not look up. His hands did the work they had been doing when she walked in — the float bowl in his left, the needle valve in his right, his thumb seating the valve at a pressure the wrist had learned somewhere she had not watched him learn it. Today&#x27;s t-shirt was faded blue, not the grease-spotted white from the hood of the pickup.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> You lost?</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She shook her head.
