Cookie had shown her that the second Thursday — string under the string, not over — and it had taken her three shifts to get it and a week past that to do it without her hands needing her eyes for the doing. The Tuesday was her seventh T0 and the first one she had walked in to without checking the chalkboard for the ticket count.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/tier_c/diner_rhythm_deepens/base_pete_coffee.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>Tuesday 5:18pm at the diner counter. She set it at his right elbow at the second booth from the end. He nodded once. She slid it under the base. The fifty-two went into the apron pocket at her hip at the seam, the weight a clean small compact thing that had a shape now.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> You&#x27;re good.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Cookie did not look up from the wheel to say it. The hook was still Cookie&#x27;s, and the hook was still Marge&#x27;s, because the diner was not hers, because she had not earned the key yet.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: location</em></div> </div> <div class="review-back-btn"> <<button "← Back to List">><<goto "CanvasReviewList">><</button>> </div> </div><div id="canvas-review-detail" data-canvas-id="the_math" data-game-name="output"> <h2>The Math</h2> <p class="canvas-id-display">Canvas ID: <code>the_math</code></p> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Desk</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/the_math/base_desk_calculator.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A teenage girl&#x27;s bedroom desk at nine-thirty at night in a southern farmhouse — lit only by a small ceramic nightstand lamp with a blue band at the base. A phone with a calculator app open on the wood desk next to a small stack of bills (ones, fives, one twenty) and a brochure folded to a page. An open notebook with handwritten figures. Window cracked two inches. Quiet late-summer interior.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The second Sunday she had been at the house was the Sunday she did the math. It was late — nine-twenty-eight by the alarm clock on the nightstand — and the house was at its Sunday-night register, which was Frank already up the stairs for the newspaper crossword and Diana at the sink rinsing the last of the glasses and the television off and the percolator off and the light under Ryan&#x27;s door not yet on because Ryan had not come back from wherever the pickup had been since seven. The cicadas were already in their nighttime count. The oscillating fan on the dresser was off. She had clicked the ceramic nightstand lamp on, the one with the chipped blue band at the base, and the light it put on the desk was the light of a 40-watt bulb in a lamp with a shade that had been cream-colored once and was now the yellow shades got when they had been in a room that had had a summer in it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She had her apron folded flat on the corner of the desk. She took the money out of the apron pocket. She put it on the desk. She took the money out from under the lamp — the cash she had put there on Friday night because putting it under the lamp had felt like putting it somewhere that meant she was keeping it — and added it to the stack. She counted it twice. She counted it the second time because the first count had been wrong in the direction she had expected it to be wrong, which was lower than her estimate. The second count was the same as the first.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>A twenty. Three fives. Four ones. Nineteen dollars more in quarters and dimes from two days of tips and one breakfast she had not bought a coffee for. Thirty-eight ones in the stack from Wednesday and Thursday&#x27;s shifts — which had been four hours Wednesday and five hours Thursday. Marge had her on the schedule for four shifts the next week, which was four more than the four she had done this week. She knew the bill in her pocket from the first paid Sunday was gone already. She had handed the first rent to Frank on the kitchen table this afternoon at three. Frank had taken it without counting in front of her and had written *Maya — Wk 1* on a small notepad from the drawer by the phone and had not said anything else about it.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She opened the calculator app on the phone. The phone was the same phone. The thumb already knew the math before the app did.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Rent was sixty a week. Summer was the summer — she had twelve Sundays left counting this one as paid. Sixty times twelve was seven-twenty. Personal things — a tube of the toothpaste she used, the kind of tampon the local pharmacy carried, a gallon of gas a week to go into town and back because the car was the car — she had put at ten a week. Ten times twelve was one-twenty. The tuition she had been carrying in her head since the phone call in April was fifteen hundred. Seven-twenty plus one-twenty plus fifteen hundred was twenty-three-forty. The total she needed to get to by the Monday before classes started, which was the third week of August, was twenty-three hundred and forty dollars.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She had, at the lamp, ninety-seven dollars and change. She had a schedule for four shifts at T0 next week and Marge had not yet committed to more. A T0 shift was forty-five. Four times forty-five was one-eighty a week gross. One-eighty minus sixty for rent and ten for personal was one-ten net. One-ten times twelve was thirteen-twenty. Plus the ninety-seven in front of her. Thirteen-twenty plus ninety-seven was fourteen-seventeen.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Fourteen-seventeen against fifteen hundred was eighty-three short. That was if Marge gave her four shifts every week for twelve weeks and she did not have a single unpaid day off and she did not have one flat tire and she did not have a pair of shoes give out and she did not have a single unplanned expense. Eighty-three short was the math for the version of the summer that did not have anything go wrong.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She wrote the numbers in the notebook. She wrote them once because writing them twice was the thing you did to be sure, and she had been sure at the first writing. The notebook was the black composition one she had brought from the apartment. The page was the first page she had opened it to in six weeks. Her handwriting on the page looked like her handwriting.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The college brochure was on the nightstand next to the lamp. It had been in the glovebox since Kentucky. She had taken it out yesterday and left it there. She had not opened it. She had seen the community-college sign on Main Street on Wednesday when the walk to the diner had taken her past the turnoff and had registered the sign without going to the building. She was not going to open the brochure tonight. She was going to leave it where she had left it. The brochure was not the part of the math that was in question.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She sat at the desk with the ninety-seven in front of her and the thirteen-twenty in the phone and the fourteen-seventeen in the notebook and the fifteen hundred that she had been carrying since April, and she did what she had been doing since she was eight and doing math at a table was a thing she did the way some other children learned to swim: she looked at the numbers and she let the numbers tell her what the numbers were saying.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The numbers were saying that the T0 column was eighty-three short in the best case, and that Marge&#x27;s Tuesday comment — *Thursdays are different. We&#x27;ll see about those.* — had been a piece of information Maya had heard without yet understanding what she was hearing. The Thursday shift paid more. The why of the paying-more had been in the way Cookie had said *if you can hold an eye* on her second day, off-hand on the floor between the pass and the counter, without explaining what the holding meant. The holding-an-eye had been a sentence Maya had filed at the back of the drawer at the time. The holding-an-eye was going to be a sentence she was going to pick up, tonight, and hold in the hand the twenty and the three fives were on the desk under.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>*There&#x27;s more tier available if I want it. I can see where it goes from here.*</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She did not open the sketchbook. The sketchbook was on the desk — was under the notebook, actually, where she had put it two nights ago for no particular reason she had named to herself at the time — and the opening of it right now would have been the opening of the register that had drawn the flat-dumpling chicken and her mother&#x27;s hands and the pine-log on the trail-head half a mile off the porch. The sketchbook was not the register the closing of the math belonged to. She left the sketchbook closed. She put the ninety-seven back in the stack. She put the stack under the lamp. She turned the lamp off. The house at nine-forty-one on a second Sunday in July did what houses did.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: location</em></div> </div> <div class="review-back-btn"> <<button "← Back to List">><<goto "CanvasReviewList">><</button>> </div> </div><div id="canvas-review-detail" data-canvas-id="first_sunday" data-game-name="output"> <h2>First Sunday</h2> <p class="canvas-id-display">Canvas ID: <code>first_sunday</code></p> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Sixty for Frank</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/first_sunday/rent_envelope_kitchen_table.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A sunlit Sunday morning kitchen in a southern farmhouse. Three twenty-dollar bills laid side by side on a worn kitchen table, beside a small brown manila envelope with handwritten &#x27;Wk 2&#x27; in pencil on the front. A folded white waitress apron with hip stains hangs over the back of a wooden chair. On the counter behind, a Mr. Coffee percolator and a cast-iron pan with bacon grease cooling. A handwritten note on the back of an envelope tucked under a salt shaker. Window cracked behind the sink with morning light coming through and basil leaves visible on the sill outside.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The note was on the counter under the salt shaker. Diana had written it on the back of the gas-bill envelope from Friday with the felt-tip pen she kept in the drawer by the toaster. The handwriting was the hand Maya had grown up reading on lunch-bag notes and refrigerator-door reminders for fourteen years before the apartment in Lexington and the year she had been on her own.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>&lt;blockquote&gt;Leave sixty for Frank before church. — D.&lt;/blockquote&gt;</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She read it once. She read it twice. The reading-twice was the small pause her body had taken without asking, the way it had taken the small pause at the calculator app two Sunday-nights from now would also be a small pause it would take. Soft early morning light through a window over the sink.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She came down the fourteen stairs in yesterday&#x27;s clothes. She had slept on top of the quilt with the jeans on and the t-shirt from the drive still on, and she had not opened the suitcase yet. The clock on the nightstand had said six-fifty-two when she had sat up. The house was already awake. The smell of coffee had been coming up the stairwell since somewhere before six-fifty-two, and had been part of what had woken her, and the other part had been the sound of the paper being opened at a table a man had been sitting at for already most of an hour.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The kitchen faced east. The light through the window over the sink was the light of a southern Sunday in July at seven in the morning, which was a light that had not yet decided whether the day was going to be the kind of hot that made the porch the cooler place than the kitchen or the kind of hot that made every room equally unusable by three. She had a coffee mug in her left hand and a kitchen towel in her right and she was wiping a spot on the counter that did not need to be wiped, which was a thing Maya was going to learn Diana did when the thing Diana was waiting on was a person not a pan. She did not smile — the smile was reserved for a second later — and she looked at Maya for the count of a mother looking at a daughter who had slept in yesterday&#x27;s clothes after a three-hundred-and-twenty-mile drive.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Sit.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Frank was at the table. The looking-back-at-the-paper was not rudeness; it was the register of a man giving a woman in his kitchen the count she was going to need to cross from the doorway to a chair without being watched for the crossing.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Diana slid a mug in front of the chair Maya had not chosen yet. The mug had *Hayes Hardware* on it in a faded blue block letter and was the mug Frank&#x27;s lumberyard had given out at an anniversary three counties over that Maya would not learn the story of for another month. The coffee was stronger than what Maya made for herself out of the grocery can of Maxwell House; it was stronger than what Diana had made when Maya was small; the summer had put something into the mornings that the coffee had risen to meet. Maya sat. She held the mug. She did not drink yet.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Frank folded the paper. He took a long breath through his nose and let it out, which was a thing he did when he was about to say a sentence whose shape he had already decided on, and he looked up over the top of the reading glasses.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Maya. The you-can-not was said at exactly the volume of the you-can-come, which was the register of a man who had decided a long time ago how to offer a daughter her own mind on a Sunday morning in a house where he was going to need her to know that he was not going to weigh the answer. Diana had not turned around.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>I&#x27;ll come.</li><li>I&#x27;ll stay.</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-back-btn"> <<button "← Back to List">><<goto "CanvasReviewList">><</button>> </div> </div><div id="canvas-review-detail" data-canvas-id="arrival_at_franks" data-game-name="output"> <h2>Arrival</h2> <p class="canvas-id-display">Canvas ID: <code>arrival_at_franks</code></p> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Gravel</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/arrival_at_franks/n1_car_on_gravel.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>A young woman&#x27;s ten-year-old sedan parked on a gravel drive in front of a two-story Southern farmhouse at five in the afternoon in July. Red-clay dust on the rear tire wells. Screen door of the porch starting to open. Cicadas implied by the angle of heat shimmer off the hood.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The last mile of Route 9 had been the long one — pines tighter on both sides than she&#x27;d remembered from visits before the move, the radio dropped to one station that was a preacher at the end of his voice, the heat built up over four hours of interstate and one hour of county two-lane until the AC had stopped being a thing she could meaningfully adjust. The turn onto the drive came up on the left after the mailbox with the name she had not yet practiced saying in her own mouth. The tires took the gravel with a sound she remembered from somewhere older than this year.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>She parked. She did not turn the engine off right away. The cicadas in the pines on the far side of the yard were into their five-in-the-afternoon count. Something frying in a neighbor&#x27;s kitchen — chicken, or okra, or the particular Saturday smell of two of those together — carried across the far fence. The clay in the drive had dried to a red she had remembered wrong since the last visit: it was redder than memory.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The house was two stories. She did not wait on the top step; she came all the way to the gravel. Diana smelled of laundry soap — the cheap grocery kind — and of basil from the side garden, and of something warmer than either that was in the skin of her neck behind the ear and had been Maya&#x27;s mother&#x27;s smell for as long as Maya had been old enough to register a mother-smell.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Maya hugged back at the weight of a daughter who had been three hundred and twenty miles on her own with the Prologue in her body. He had come out of the kitchen at the sound of Diana&#x27;s voice and had stopped at the jamb, one hand flat on it at shoulder height, the other in his pocket. He had shaved that afternoon. The face was the same face and was not; the line at the left corner of the mouth had been less deep the last time. He looked at her. He held the look for the count he held looks for.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Maya.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He said her name at the volume a man said a name at when the name was the full sentence he had to say. The sentence the moment required.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He came down the two steps. He offered his hand for the suitcase — offering hand as the sentence. He turned toward the door.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Diana&#x27;s hand was at the small of Maya&#x27;s back, guiding her toward the steps. The hand did not push. The inside of the hall was cooler.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: choices</em><ul><li>Inside.</li></ul></div> </div> <div class="review-node"> <h4>NODE: Hallway</h4> <div class="review-block review-block-image"><img src="./videos/story/arrival_at_franks/n3_upstairs_hall_bedroom_door.jpg" style="max-width:100%;max-height:70vh;object-fit:contain;height:auto;border-radius:8px;" /><p class="media-caption"><em>Upstairs hallway of a two-story Southern farmhouse with a runner carpet, a bathroom door standing open across from a bedroom door, suitcase being set inside the bedroom, late-afternoon light through a hall window at the end. Warm domestic late-summer interior.</em></p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>The hall ran front to back with the staircase on the right, the living room on the left, and the kitchen through the dining-room arch at the far end. Maya counted the stairs because counting stairs on first climbs was a thing she had done since she was small. They were fourteen.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Frank turned left at the top. He set the suitcase inside the door of the second room on the left — the room Diana had told her about over the phone on the Sunday in April. An oscillating fan on the dresser, off. The runner in the hall ended at the door frame; past that the floor was bare wood.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Bathroom&#x27;s across the hall. Dinner&#x27;s at six-thirty.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Both sentences at the minimum length — the first a piece of information she could have found on her own, the second a piece of the ritual she was now inside. From the window, before Maya had set her hand to any of the things in the room, a voice came up through the screen from the yard — through the two-inch gap the way voices carried on summer afternoons in the South.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Hey, kid.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Two syllables from a man who did not come inside to say them. A voice she would place later, on the second day, as Ryan&#x27;s. Tonight she placed it only as a man&#x27;s voice from a yard at arm&#x27;s length through a screen. She did not go to the window. She did not answer. The voice was the sentence; the sentence had been said; the protocol was to let it have been said.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Dinner at six-thirty was in the dining room through the arch from the kitchen. The table was set for five. Diana at the head. Frank at the foot. Ryan was at the side of the table facing the kitchen — he had come in from the yard sometime between the suitcase going upstairs and the plates going on the table. She registered first his hands (on the table, knuckled and clean at the knuckle and tanned past it) and then the rest of him in the second pass. He said hey at the volume of a man who had already said it through a screen and was not going to repeat himself.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Jake was across from Ryan. Black t-shirt. Headphones around his neck, cord into the pocket of jeans older than Ryan&#x27;s. Glasses off. He was looking at his plate before food was on it — the looking of a person who had chosen the plate over the room. Diana came to his chair and said his name once.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-dialog"><blockquote><strong>npc:</strong> Jake.</blockquote></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>He nodded. He did not look up. The nod was the whole meeting — not rudeness exactly but the register of a boy who had decided the telling had been enough preparation. Diana served him. She did not say his name again.</p></div> <div class="review-block review-block-paragraph"><p>Dinner was brief. The food was good. Nobody asked Maya about the drive. Frank asked Ryan about a part for the mower; Ryan answered in a fragment. Diana cleared before the table was empty. Maya was in bed by eight with her door closed. She closed it quietly. She lay on the quilt with her clothes on and listened to a house that was going to be her house — the percolator getting put away, the television at low volume in the living room, a truck down on Route 9 changing gears, the cicadas through her two-inch-cracked window — and the fact, which she did not yet have a name for, that she had crossed a threshold she was not going to cross back across.</p></div> <div class="exit-info"><em>Exit: location</em></div> </div> <div class="review-back-btn"> <<button "← Back to List">><<goto "CanvasReviewList">><</button>> </div> </div>
